cia-0000124269: A November 1957 CIA item examines an alleged Czech contribution to the launching of Sputnik. In the shock after the first satellite, every rumor about who had helped Moscow drew attention. The item records the claim together with the agency's interest in it. cia-0000119769: An August 1956 CIA item reports Hungarian writers demanding freedom of expression. Writers and debating circles were turning into a force for revolt that summer. The item captures that ferment months before the uprising, when poets were already testing the regime's limits. Writers moved first in many East European crises, since their unions and journals gave private discontent a public voice before parties or crowds could act openly.
cia-0000126869: An October 1979 CIA review of Near East and South Asia affairs gives the outlook for the insurgency in Afghanistan, the heading breaking off. Rebels were rising against the communist government in Kabul, and the Soviet invasion was two months away. The review forecasts the rebellion's course. Within two months Soviet troops crossed the border, and this October outlook became a baseline for judging how well the agency had read the rebellion.
cia-0000132169: Numbered 487 in the January 1991 Iraq-Kuwait series, this situation report covers political developments and an Iraqi terrorist matter the heading cuts off. Saddam's threats of terror were meant to split the coalition facing him. The report follows both tracks. Terror threats ran through the whole crisis winter, and each sitrep touching them fed the guarding of embassies, bases, and airlines across three continents.
cia-0000132569: Closer cultural ties between East Germany and Cuba fill a CIA item dated October 1, 1960. Culture was following trade and arms into the Soviet orbit that year. East Berlin was becoming the bloc's cultural outpost in Havana, hosting visits and exchanges. The short item notes the new ties as one more strand in Cuba's turn toward the communist world.
cia-0000132669: Latin American reactions to the Cuban situation fill a CIA paper dated January 2, 1961. The American break with Havana was about to land, and every capital was setting its position in advance. The region's response was itself the story that week. The short paper gathers the reactions from across the hemisphere as they reached analysts in the first days of the year.
cia-0000132769: Three strands of the Cuban situation share a CIA paper dated June 4, 1960. One strand covers money deals with the bloc. A second covers a Latin American youth congress. The headline breaks off before the list is done. Money and youth were two of the revolution's chief tools abroad. The short paper takes the roundup strand by strand.
cia-0000134269: Communists spreading work based in Cuba across the region fill item 16 of the CIA's Latin America series. The item is dated February 3, 1960. Its headline breaks off before the region's name is done. Havana was becoming the base from which the left worked across the hemisphere. The short item tracks that spread and its agents.
cia-0000135869: A planning paper of 5 November 1952 survives in the declassified CIA files, dealing with the current planning of the Calligeris organization, with attachments holding the detail. Behind the paper stands PBSUCCESS, the covert CIA campaign against President Arbenz that closed with the 1954 coup in Guatemala. Records like this one let the operation be studied from the inside, in the terms its own staff used.
cia-0000135969: The open CIA files hold a cable dated 3 January 1954 that deals with the scanning of student personnel records, raw material for the recruiting of new assets. As the Lincoln station file, it forms part of PBSUCCESS, the CIA plan that ended with President Arbenz driven out in June 1954. Its worth is in the detail it pins down, one dated piece of a covert war fought largely on paper.
cia-0000136069: Dated 1 March 1954, a declassified CIA cable deals with preventing red penetration, guarding the operation against communist agents inside its own ranks. In these files Lincoln names the field station of PBSUCCESS, the covert CIA plan to topple President Arbenz of Guatemala. The heading alone tells a reader the topic, the channel, and the moment, even where names stay deleted.
cia-0000136169: A CIA cable from 6 April 1954, now declassified, deals with WSBURNT military matters, cabled to PAGE in the first week of April 1954. In these files Lincoln names the field station of PBSUCCESS, the covert CIA plan to topple President Arbenz of Guatemala. What survives is the working paper itself, plain proof of how the mission was run from day to day.
cia-0000136269: A CIA situation report dated 1 May 1954 deals with daily situation report number 06, the numbered heartbeat of the operation in May, in files since declassified. The paper sits inside the CIA drive against President Arbenz, run under the code name PBSUCCESS and crowned by the June 1954 coup. Its worth is in the detail it pins down, one dated piece of a covert war fought largely on paper.
cia-0000136369: SKIMMER should contact CALLIGERIS soonest, LINCOLN urges in this June 1954 cable, to establish a plausible and palatable explanation of his air support for the liberation movement. The cover story offered: one fighter aircraft crash-landed and is being held, and another will shortly be brought in. To enact it, CALLIGERIS should send a trusted pilot within days to SOMERSET to pick up one F-47, with Mendoza recommended. Deception here is routine staff work.
cia-0000136969: Stick to the facts, headquarters tells LINCOLN in this May 1954 cable about BRODFROST advising STORAX of a plane flight. A Venezuelan plane flying a secret mission over Central America has been reported; in any message to BRODFROST, avoid any hint of our exploitation of this development. The station should use the New York Times intercept report plus specified details from a reference message, which are best treated as factual. The cable coaches careful talk about another country's covert flight.
cia-0000137469: Venezuela's extremists are active but contained in these late 1961 reports. They were written ahead of Kennedy's visit. Anti-government flysheets were spread outside a Caracas theater. Anti-Kennedy flysheets appeared too. No violent disturbances took place. As of 10 December, no extremist leaders had been detained. The government had not decided on detaining those with congressional immunity. Guards were posted around Dutch businesses. In Zulia, the Movement of the Revolutionary Left plans a December revolt. The Communist Party refused to join it.
cia-0000139169: Daily diary excerpts from the photo interpretation center record autumn 1978 work. A requisition for Kodak film and paper was approved. It was returned through channels. cia-0000139369: Terms of reference for National Intelligence Estimate 11-4-61, Main Trends in Soviet Capabilities and Policies 1961-1965, are forwarded in this May 1961 memorandum from Acting Deputy Assistant Director Willard Matthias. Representatives are asked to meet on 12 June in the Administration Building to discuss the terms, covering annexes A and B. The surviving sample is the routing memorandum, not the estimate's judgments themselves. It shows the machinery by which the intelligence community framed its five-year Soviet forecast at the Cold War's Berlin-crisis moment.
un-ga-res-a-69-69:
A world pact to ban the use of nuclear arms is urged in Resolution A/69/69, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. The text holds that the use of such arms is the gravest threat to the life of mankind. It recalls the 1996 ruling of the International Court of Justice on the law of nuclear threat and use. Some cuts by Russia and the United States are noted with care.

A shared, binding pact that bars the use or threat of nuclear arms, the Assembly argues, would help clear the nuclear threat away. It would set the stage for talks toward the full end of such arms. The vote keeps alive a long push, led by states with no nuclear arms of their own.
un-sc-res-369: Kept in the official record of the United Nations, Security Council Resolution 369 is catalogued here as dating from 1975. Voting in the Council requires support from its permanent members, so each adopted text marks a point of agreement. Readers will find the full wording here, taken from the English Wikisource transcription of the UN official record. The entry belongs to the library's DECLASSIFIED group of public official records.
un-sc-res-969: A formal decision of the United Nations Security Council, Resolution 969 is catalogued here under 1995. The Council's fifteen members vote on draft texts, and adopted ones enter the record as numbered resolutions. The library holds the complete text in the form transcribed for English Wikisource from the official UN record. As a public record, it has long been open to scholars and general readers alike.
un-sc-res-1269: The United Nations Security Council issued Resolution 1269 as one of its formal decisions, and the catalog carries it under the year 1999. Year by year, these decisions build the written history of how the world body handled the crises of its time. The transcription keeps the preamble and numbered clauses in their official order, as the Council adopted them.
cia-0000136769: The catalog gives this Spanish text from the 2506 Brigade documents an estimated date of 1 January 1961. The brigade was then training in secret for the invasion of Cuba. un-ga-res-34-169:
General Assembly Resolution 34/169, adopted on December 17, 1979, set out a Code of Conduct for Law Enforcement Officials. The first number marks the Assembly's thirty-fourth session, which fixes the year; catalog entries dating it to 1966 are in error. Every member state received the code with a request to write it into national law and police training.

Eight short articles tell officers to serve the public, guard human rights, and use force only when strictly needed. Torture and cruel treatment are banned outright, and officers must shield the health of people in custody. The code also bars corruption and orders respect for the law even in hard cases. It remains a basic yardstick for police conduct worldwide.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d69: A second message from Churchill to Roosevelt dated October 29, 1943 stands as Document 69 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Splitting the day's business into two notes was the prime minister's habit when matters differed in kind. The record does not say what set this note apart from its companion. Both are printed in the Foreign Relations series, in the pause between the Moscow Conference and the November summits.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d169: A second letter from Roosevelt to Hull is dated October 26, 1943, and it stands as Document 169 of the Cairo and Tehran volume, in the Moscow Conference section. Two presidential letters to his secretary in one day, across an ocean and a war, kept the home government's hand firm on the talks. The record names the parties and the date. The letter's text is printed in the Foreign Relations series.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d269:
Minutes of the Combined Chiefs of Staff meeting at Cairo on 25 November 1943, at half past two in the afternoon, take up Southeast Asia operations. Admiral Mountbatten reports his meeting of the day before with Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek on the Burma campaign plan.

Chiang had insisted on the larger plan, for which the resources did not exist. It needed 535 more transport aircraft. He settled for the smaller one once the chiefs were formally asked for the planes. He also demanded a seaborne operation alongside the land advance in north Burma. On airlift over the Hump, he held out for the full 10,000 tons a month against a promised average of 8,900. Mountbatten asks for Chiang's agreement to the campaign in writing.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d369:
Minutes of the Combined Chiefs of Staff meeting at Tehran on 30 November 1943 record a morning session at half past nine. The Western staffs were trying to agree a basis for that afternoon's plenary session with the Soviets. Landing craft, once again, decide nearly every question.

Brooke proposes a sequence. Italy comes first, with Eisenhower keeping his landing craft until 15 January to reach the Pisa-Rimini line. Rhodes follows only if Turkey enters the war. Then comes the south of France, with craft from Rhodes returning in time. Leahy answers that the whole knot is Overlord's date: the Russians want it fixed in May, and if that date stands, other operations must fit around it. The British doubt the returning craft can be repaired and their crews trained in time, and ask for American repair facilities.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d469:
President Roosevelt wrote to President Bishara al-Khouri of Lebanon on December 3, 1943, during the conference season at Cairo. Lebanon had just come through a crisis in November, when French authorities arrested its leaders and then released them under pressure, leaving Lebanese independence recognized in fact. The letter appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume.

Roosevelt's message reached a small new state sitting at the center of Allied supply lines and Arab politics. American interest in Lebanon mixed wartime logistics with sympathy for independence from the French mandate. For readers, the letter shows the President tending ties far beyond the Big Three table where the cameras pointed.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d569:

frus-1944-quebec-d69:

frus-1945-malta-yalta-d169:

frus-1945-malta-yalta-d269:

In-context learning folds cloth instantly. Yilong Wang taught robots to fold cloth. Home robotics needs deformable manipulation. Wang's Instant-Fold speeds laundry robots.
arxiv-2606-04469: Adaptive calibration was developed for fair and performant facial recognition. The fairness method was engineered. The finding serves AI ethics. Adaptive calibration balances fairness and accuracy. Ryan Brown calibrated facial recognition fairly. Biometric deployment needs fairness calibration. Brown's calibration reduces biometric bias.
arxiv-2606-04669: SoK: post-quantum cryptography implementation in software systems was systematized. The systematization was written. The finding serves cybersecurity. PQC migration needs systematized knowledge. Shakya systematized PQC migration knowledge. Critical infrastructure needs PQC roadmaps. Shakya's SoK prepares quantum-safe migration. Shakya's systematization guides CISOs.
arxiv-2606-05069: Mastodon is social media with no central owner — thousands of independent servers, each with its own rules. This paper studies how community governance scales across those instances: who makes the rules, how they are enforced, and what breaks as servers grow. It is a field guide to running a federated social network without a corporate overlord.
arxiv-2606-05169: A benchmark tests only a slice of what a language model can do, the way a 2D slice reveals only part of a 3D object. Borrowing stereology — the science of inferring wholes from slices — this paper builds a theory of benchmark coverage, quantifying the blind spots every evaluation leaves. It gives the AI field a principled way to ask what its tests are not measuring.
arxiv-2606-05269: X-ray beam-tracking microscopy watches how X-rays bend through a sample to reveal its inner structure. This paper studies the technique's spatial resolution — the finest detail it can distinguish. Understanding resolution limits tells scientists exactly what questions this imaging method can and cannot answer.
arxiv-2606-05469: At the Large Hadron Collider, near-miss collisions of lead nuclei flood the detectors with photons that can birth charm quarks. This paper studies diffractive open charm photoproduction in ultraperipheral lead-lead and proton-lead collisions — photon-driven physics at energies no laser could reach. The measurements probe the gluon-dense heart of matter.
arxiv-2606-05769: Predicting what happens next in a video is easier if you first imagine it. This paper interleaves latent visual reasoning with prediction — imagine, then predict, then imagine again — for video event forecasting. Structured imagination beats blind extrapolation when anticipating events.
arxiv-2606-06169: Phase-field models simulate cracks growing through materials — but real materials break by their own strength criteria. This paper endows variational phase-field fracture models with custom strength criteria, letting engineers encode how their material actually fails. Custom fracture physics makes virtual testing trustworthy.
arxiv-2606-06369: Scene graphs — structured descriptions of images — improve when the model knows visual commonsense. This paper refines scene graph generation with visual commonsense-driven knowledge: cups sit on tables, not ceilings. Commonsense keeps generated graphs grounded in how the world works.
arxiv-2606-06669: Sidon sets — numbers with all-distinct pairwise sums — can sometimes be decomposed into simpler pieces. This paper tackles the Sidon decomposition problem in abelian groups of bounded torsion. The decomposition reveals hidden structure in these extremal sets of integers.
arxiv-2606-06469: Machine learning loves interpolators — models that fit training data exactly. But how abundant are good ones? This paper asks how many interpolating functions actually generalize well. The answer reshapes how we think about overfitting. Not all interpolators are created equal.
arxiv-2606-06769: Testing hypotheses sequentially — as data arrives — with constraints is statistically delicate. This paper develops sequential testing for conditionally constrained hypotheses. The methods let experimenters stop early without cheating. The framework respects statistical constraints while letting curiosity guide the stopping.
arxiv-2606-07169: Posterior predictive checks test Bayesian models — but can they identify the learning rate? This paper answers exactly when, with exact degeneracy results in Gaussian models. The answer clarifies what model checks can reveal. Model checks have limits. The theory clarifies what they reveal.
arxiv-2606-00069: LiDAR segmentation for self-driving needs uncertainty awareness. Invascal self-calibrates with inverse-vacuity for range-view semantic segmentation. The calibration knows when the sensor is unsure. Automotive sensors must know their limits. Proper calibration enables genuinely safe autonomy. Safety cannot ever be compromised.
tob-10469:
Aquinas turns from God to human life in Part I-II of the Summa, the first half of its second part. The subject is how people act and why. Happiness, the will, good and evil in actions, and the passions all come under his question-and-answer method.

Habits receive close attention: how repeated acts become virtues or vices, and what roles law and grace play in making a life good. Aquinas maps the moral life with an engineer's care, defining terms before judging cases. Readers meet the framework behind centuries of Catholic ethics, including ideas about natural law that later reached far beyond the church.
tob-10969:
The complete Douay-Rheims Bible joins the Old Testament translated at Douai in 1609 with the New Testament translated at Rheims in 1582, in Bishop Richard Challoner's eighteenth-century revision. Challoner modernized spelling and softened the most Latin-heavy phrasing, producing the text most later readers know. For three hundred years this was the English Bible of Catholics worldwide.

From Genesis to Revelation, the translation stays formal and Latinate, close to the Vulgate that stood behind it. Psalms and Gospels alike carry the wording generations of Catholics prayed from memory. Traditionalists still favor it, and readers comparing English Bibles will find its differences from the King James Version instructive.
tob-0169:
Joseph Andrew Blackwell's translation presents the Elder Eddas, the old Norse poems associated with Saemund Sigfusson, alongside material from the Younger Edda of Snorri Sturluson. Gods and heroes speak in their own stark verse. Odin's gallows-wisdom in the Hávamál, the seeress's prophecy of Ragnarök, and the lays of Sigurd stand among the highlights.

These poems, preserved in Icelandic manuscripts, are the wellspring of Norse mythology: creation from a giant's body, the world tree, and the gods' foreknown doom at the twilight. Blackwell's version keeps their power in older English dress. Readers who know Norse myth only through retellings will find the originals stranger, funnier, and more fatalistic.
galton-hereditary-genius-1869:
Francis Galton published Hereditary Genius in 1869, his first book on inherited ability. He collected the family histories of judges, statesmen, scientists, and other eminent men. Patterns in those pedigrees drive his whole argument.

Galton claims that talent clusters in families because nature outweighs training. He ranks relatives by closeness and counts how eminence fades with distance. The inquiry launched the nature-versus-nurture debate in modern form. It also launched eugenics, whose harms readers must keep in view. The statistical ambition was real; so were the blind spots. Galton later expanded its methods into the statistical study of human differences generally.
brasseur-manuscrit-troano-vol-1-1869:
One of the few Maya books to survive the conquest came to print in 1869. Manuscrit Troano, volume one, is Brasseur de Bourbourg's first publication of the Troano Codex. The French edition opened the painted manuscript to the scholars of Europe.

Brasseur prints the codex pages and begins his study of Maya script and tongue. He read the signs as a tale of land lost to the sea, a reading few now accept. From his misreading, Le Plongeon later drew the name Mu for a sunken land. The volume still marks the birth of Troano study.
bolender-draft-1969:
Blue Book shut in 1969, but the Air Force still had to field UFO reports that touched national safety. The Bolender Draft, a memo of October 20, 1969, from General Carroll Bolender, lays out how. It tells which reports should still move up a sealed chain.

Bolender writes that reports which bear on the safety of the nation are not part of the Blue Book system. They were to be handled by other Air Force paths once the public program died. The draft shows the quiet afterlife of the UFO desk. It has fed years of debate on what the service kept back.
blue-book-termination-1969:
The Air Force signed the death warrant of its UFO study on December 17, 1969. News Release 1077-69, from Secretary Robert Seamans, tells the world Project Blue Book is done. Twenty years of files, sightings, and public mail end with this one plain sheet.

The release holds that the study could not be backed on grounds of national safety or of science. No case in the files, it says, shows craft past the skill of earth. The words are dry and flat, and the effect was vast. Blue Book's end is the hinge of the whole government UFO tale.
catoe-ufo-bibliography-1969:
Lynn Catoe of the Library of Congress mapped the whole UFO shelf in 1969. UFOs and Related Subjects is her annotated bibliography, made for the Air Force Office of Scientific Research. The book runs to 417 pages of entries and notes.

Books, reports, and magazine work stand in neat ranks, each with a fair word on its worth. Catoe wastes no awe and no scorn; her tone is that of a guide, not a judge. The volume shows how vast the UFO field had grown by the end of Blue Book. It stays the standard map of that field.
randolph-pre-adamite-man-1869:
Paschal Beverly Randolph claimed man is far more old than the Good Book says in Pre-Adamite Man, out in 1869. Bands of men, he held, lived and built on earth long ere Adam. He draws on stone tools, old bones, and tales from the East to make his bold case for deep time.

The claim was hot stuff in his day. Church men balked, while men of the dig cheered parts of it. Randolph gives the claim an occult spin all his own. The book is his word in a great row of his age. Stone finds in his day had just begun to shake old views. Randolph seized on them fast to back his claim of man's deep age.
randolph-love-and-its-hidden-history-186:
Paschal Beverly Randolph wrote of love as a force of fate in Love and Its Hidden History, out in 1869. He held that love binds souls by laws as strict as those of the stars. A wrong bond can blight a life. A right one can lift both souls to health and sight.

Rules, tales, and warns fill the book. It is the hands-on mate to his later Eulis! Fans who sought his lore in full read the pair as one. The book shows his warm, grave voice at its best. Randolph wed twice and knew love's joys and griefs at first hand. That past gives his grave rules a warmth texts of law lack.
sargent-planchette-1869:
Epes Sargent took up arms for the faith in Planchette, his book of 1869. Its flip name calls science to scorn: The Despair of Science. The planchette was a small board on wheels that spelled words in the dark room. Sargent, a news man, holds that its words mock the cold creed that all is mere stuff and force.

He prints cases, talks with the dead, and sharp words for his foes. His aim is to show the lab has no key for these doors. The book is the faith's best fight back of its age in his land.
dunraven-experiences-spiritualism-home-1:
Lord Adare kept a log of dark nights in Experiences in Spiritualism with Mr. D. D. Home, out in 1869. Adare, heir to an earl, sat with Home through 1867 to 1869. He writes each night's feats as they came: sounds, moves, forms, and a famed float past the panes of a high room in London town.

His rank and calm tone gave the tales great weight. The log was meant for a small ring, yet soon roamed wide. It is the best guest's eye tale of the top seer at work. Doubt it or not, it grips.
arnold-culture-anarchy-1869:
Matthew Arnold published Culture and Anarchy in 1869, a set of essays on English society. Arnold defines culture as the pursuit of perfection through knowledge of the best that has been thought and said. Against culture he sets anarchy: each person doing as he likes without shared standards. He sorts England into Barbarians, Philistines, and Populace by class.

Sweetness and light is his shorthand for beauty and intelligence joined. The book became the founding text of modern cultural criticism in English. Arnold's urbane wit softens a serious call for public standards. Debates about culture and education still start from his terms. It is his most famous prose work.
mill-subjection-women-1869:
John Stuart Mill published The Subjection of Women in 1869, a founding text of liberal feminism. Mill argues that the legal subordination of women is wrong in itself and bad for society. What is called women's nature, he says, is an artificial product of forced repression. No one can know women's capacities until they are free.

He demands equal education, equal access to work, and the vote. The argument proceeds from utility and justice together. Mill credited many ideas to his wife, Harriet Taylor Mill. The book scandalized many Victorian readers. It remains a model of clear, principled argument for equality.
lecky-european-morals-1869:
W. E. H. Lecky published History of European Morals in 1869, a classic Victorian study of moral ideas. Lecky traces how standards of right and wrong changed from the Roman Empire to his own century. He treats slavery, charity, chastity, and the treatment of animals and enemies. Pagan and Christian morals are weighed in turn.

Lecky writes with calm learning and wide reading in primary sources. He credits Christianity with raising charity, yet faults its record on tolerance and the intellect. The book became the standard history of morals for generations. Its method shaped later work on the history of ideas. It remains clear, fair, and absorbing.
wallace-malay-archipelago-1869:
Alfred Russel Wallace spent eight years in the islands of Malaysia and Indonesia collecting birds, insects, and mammals. His 1869 book The Malay Archipelago tells that journey in full. He supported himself by selling specimens to museums and collectors back home. He wrote it after he and Darwin had jointly announced natural selection.

Wallace describes volcanoes, jungles, rare birds of paradise, and the peoples who guided and fed him. He also notes a sharp line dividing the islands' animal life, still called Wallace's Line by scientists. The narrative mixes danger, illness, and wonder with calm, exact observation. The book remains a founding story of biogeography, the study of where species live and why.
finney-character-claims-of-freemasonry-1:
Charles G Finney, a leading revival preacher, published his attack on Freemasonry in 1869. Finney said he had once been a Mason himself, and he wrote as a Christian minister alarmed by the lodge. His target was not one lodge but the whole system.

Finney examined Masonic oaths, claims, and daily practice, and argued that they conflicted with Christian faith and honest public life. He warned that secret pledges could place a brother Mason above church, family, or court. The book became a key text for evangelical critics, and it shows how sharp the clash between revival faith and lodge loyalty could be.
beguin-tyrocinium-chymicum-1669:
Jean Béguin's Tyrocinium Chymicum, first issued in Latin in 1610, appeared in English in 1669. Béguin taught chemistry in Paris and wrote for beginners, as his title's word for a first lesson suggests. His primer was among the first clear textbooks of the new chemical art.

Lessons define terms, describe vessels and furnaces, and give recipes for medicines from plants, animals, and minerals. Béguin favored plain steps over the riddles of older alchemical writers. Students across Europe learned from the book for decades. It shows chemistry stepping away from secret symbols toward teaching that any trained reader could follow and repeat.
macoy-general-history-freemasonry-1869:
Robert Macoy published his General History, Cyclopedia and Dictionary of Freemasonry in 1869 in New York. Macoy was a major American Masonic publisher and organizer. He meant the volume as a single reference work that a lodge member or curious reader could keep at hand.

Entries cover symbols, degrees, officers, and terms, while longer sections trace the order from early guilds to modern lodges. Biographies of noted Masons and accounts of rites in many lands fill out the survey. Macoy wrote as a supporter of the craft, not a critic. The book remains a handy record of how American Masonry described itself in the nineteenth century.
agrippa-vanitie-and-uncertaintie-1569:
Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa's attack on the arts and sciences appeared in English in 1569, translated by James Sandford. The Latin original, De Vanitate, had shocked readers decades earlier. Agrippa, himself a famed scholar and occult writer, turned on the very learning he practiced.

Chapter by chapter, Agrippa mocked the claims of grammar, poetry, history, medicine, law, theology, and magic itself. He showed experts disagreeing, frauds thriving, and each art failing to give sure truth. Only faith, he argued, stood firm. The book is a great skeptical performance, half serious and half sly. It influenced later doubters and shows how deep distrust of experts ran even at the height of Renaissance learning.
wallace-malay-archipelago-vol-1-1869:
Alfred Russel Wallace published Volume 1 of The Malay Archipelago in 1869, after eight years of travel in the islands between Asia and Australia. Wallace earned his living by collecting specimens for sale. At the same time he formed, on his own, the theory of natural selection that Charles Darwin also reached.

Volume 1 follows Wallace through Singapore, Malaya, and the great islands of the west, describing forests, volcanoes, and peoples. He logged birds, insects, and mammals, and noted sharp changes in species from island to island. Those changes led to the line now called the Wallace Line. The book mixes adventure, sharp observation, and science of the first rank.
wallace-malay-archipelago-vol-2-1869:
Volume 2 of Wallace's Malay Archipelago appeared in 1869, completing his account of eight years in the islands of Southeast Asia and New Guinea. Alfred Russel Wallace had collected more than a hundred thousand specimens on the trip. The second volume moves east, toward the lands of birds of paradise.

Wallace described the Aru Islands, New Guinea, and the Moluccas, with their rare birds and distinct peoples. He compared island species on each side of a deep divide now called the Wallace Line. His notes on the bird of paradise hunts remain famous. The volume closes a travel book that is also a founding work of the study of how species are spread across the earth.
browning-ring-and-book-vol1-1869:
Robert Browning built his longest poem on a real Roman murder case from the 1690s. He found the trial records in an old book bought in Florence. The Ring and the Book came out in four volumes in 1868 and 1869, and this is the first.

The opening book explains how Browning found the records and shaped his plan. Then the voices begin: Roman gossips, the murdered woman's family, and others each tell the story their own way. A count has killed his young wife, and every witness sees the crime differently. The method lets truth emerge slowly from clashing accounts.
browning-ring-and-book-vol2-1869:
Robert Browning's long poem The Ring and the Book retells a Roman murder trial from the 1690s. He published it in four volumes across 1868 and 1869. This second volume holds Books Five through Eight of the twelve-book poem.

Each book gives the same crime to a new speaker. Here the lawyers argue, the accused count defends himself, and other voices weigh in with gossip and guesswork. No two accounts agree, and Browning trusts the reader to sort truth from self-interest. The middle volumes show his method at full stretch, turning dry court papers into living drama.
browning-ring-and-book-vol3-1869:
Robert Browning shaped The Ring and the Book from real records of a murder trial held in Rome in 1698. The poem came out in four volumes in 1868 and 1869. This third volume holds Books Nine through Eleven.

These books carry the longest and most moving speeches in the whole poem. The murdered wife, Pompilia, tells her story on her deathbed, and the priest Caponsacchi describes his attempt to rescue her. The Pope himself then weighs the case in a famous reflective speech. Together they build steadily toward the verdict that the final volume delivers at last.
browning-ring-and-book-vol4-1869:
Robert Browning closed his longest poem, The Ring and the Book, with this fourth volume, published in 1869. The poem retells a Roman murder case of 1698 through twelve separate speeches. Book Twelve, held in this volume, ends the whole design.

Browning steps forward in his own voice to judge what the many speakers have shown. He explains the gold-and-alloy image behind his title, the ring made from mixed metal and shaped by craft. Letters and reports after the trial round out the record. The ending defends the poem's method: truth found by testing many partial accounts against each other.
leger-histoire-eglises-vaudoises-1669:
Jean-Paul Léger, a Waldensian pastor, wrote the general history of the evangelical churches of the valleys of Piedmont in 1669. His own people, the Vaudois, had kept their faith in the Alpine valleys since long before the Reformation. The book is in French. Léger wrote as pastor, witness, and exile after the massacres of 1655.

The first book sets out the doctrine and discipline of the valley churches. The second tells the persecutions, rising to the Piedmontese Easter of 1655, when ducal troops slaughtered the Vaudois and Milton's sonnet cried out across Europe. Léger prints the papers and the names. His history is the founding archive of the Waldensian memory.
reid-inquiry-human-mind-1769:
Thomas Reid, a Scottish professor, published An Inquiry into the Human Mind in 1764. The edition of 1769 is the text here, carrying his principles of common sense. Reid wrote against the ideal theory, the view that the mind knows only its own ideas. David Hume had drawn bleak results from that view, and Reid aimed to answer him at the root.

Reid argues that belief in an outer world, and in other minds, rests on common sense built into human nature. Perception, on his account, reaches the world itself, not a screen of images. The Inquiry founded the Scottish common-sense school of philosophy. Its plain, sturdy method still appeals to readers tired of elegant doubt.
morgagni-sedibus-alexander-vol1-1769:
Giovanni Battista Morgagni founded pathological anatomy in De sedibus, first printed in Latin in 1761. Benjamin Alexander translated the work into English in 1769, and volume one begins the set. Morgagni compared the symptoms of the sick with the lesions found after death. His records drew on some seven hundred autopsies.

Letter by letter, he matches bedside stories to damaged organs. That matching created clinicopathological reasoning, still the core of diagnosis. Volume one opens a three volume English set. Doctors learned from it to ask where disease sits in the body. The change in thinking was enormous. Modern pathology starts on these pages.
morgagni-sedibus-alexander-vol2-1769:
Volume two of Alexander's 1769 English Morgagni continues De sedibus, the seats and causes of diseases. The first volume began Morgagni's letters matching symptoms to organ lesions. This volume carries the survey through the middle of his five Latin books. Its last page ends book three, as the original note records.

Autopsy reports pile up, each tying a case history to findings in the body. Chest, belly, and the organs between them receive their share of cases. Morgagni's method stays steady: observe, open, compare, and record. The volume forms the center of a three part set. Pathologists still honor the discipline shown here. It is heavy reading with heavy rewards.
morgagni-sedibus-alexander-vol3-1769:
Alexander's English Morgagni ends with volume three, printed in 1769 like its fellows. The Latin De sedibus of 1761 reshaped medicine by rooting disease in organs. This closing volume finishes the remaining books of cases. A general index ends the set, marked by the words The End.

Morgagni's letters complete their long survey of the body's seats of illness. Symptoms recorded in life stand matched with lesions found in death, case after case. The full English set runs to three volumes. Together they founded pathological anatomy for English readers. Few medical works of the century carried more weight. The index alone shows the scope.
borlase-antiquities-cornwall-1769:
Fifteen years after his first Cornwall volume, William Borlase brought out a second, larger edition in 1769. The Antiquities of Cornwall had grown with its author and with the county lore sent to him. Borlase revised the text, added new material, and folded in his Observations, giving the work its fullest and most settled form.

The same great subjects return: stone circles, cromlechs, and inscribed stones across the county, now more fully drawn. With more sites recorded and earlier claims rethought, the edition stands as the mature shape of his Cornish corpus. Readers who want Borlase at his most complete come to the 1769 printing rather than the first.
grettir-saga-magnusson-morris-1869:
Grettir the Strong killed a ghost, outlived a curse, and held out as an outlaw for nineteen years in Iceland. His saga, translated by Eiríkr Magnússon and William Morris in 1869, tells of strength wasted by temper and fate. Grettir could beat any man or monster, yet could not master his fear of the dark.

Hauntings, wrestling matches with the undead, and lonely winters on a sea-girt rock fill the tale. Morris loved the sagas and helped give them their English shape in versions like this one. The Story of Grettir stands as the greatest of the Icelandic family sagas in outlaw form, grim and human at once.
salmon-conic-sections-1869:
George Salmon, an Irish scholar, wrote his Treatise on Conic Sections as a textbook of analytic geometry. The 1869 edition was the standard Victorian version, used by students for decades. Salmon later became a noted churchman, but math made his name.

The book studies the ellipse, parabola, and hyperbola through algebra. Salmon shows how one set of equations can describe all three curves and their shared traits. Clear proofs and many worked cases made it a model textbook. Generations of students learned the geometry of cones and orbits from Salmon's orderly pages. Salmon treats both the pure curves and their use in the wider geometry course.
plos-pone-0003369:
Jeremy R. Sanford and co-authors published this genetics study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was SF2/ASF, a protein that helps cut and paste gene messages before use. The protein also moves back and forth between the cell nucleus and the outer cell body. The team set out to list which messages it binds in each place.

Inside, the authors explain how they pulled the protein from cells and read the RNA tied to it. They report separate target lists for the nucleus and for the outer cell body. Those lists link one protein to splicing, message export, and protein building. The work helps explain how a single factor can guide a message from gene to finished protein.
plos-pone-0003469:
Virginia Tirino and co-authors hunted stem-like cells in solid tumors for this 2008 paper. Osteosarcoma is the most common primary tumor of bone. Solid tumors mix many cell types with unlike roles. A small subset may hold stem cell powers and drive growth.

The team detected and characterized cells marked by CD133 in human tumors. Such cells may gain aggressiveness and resist treatment. Killing the root cells could stop tumors from regrowing. This survey helps define what those cancer stem cells look like. Bone tumors strike the young most often, raising the stakes of relapse.
plos-pone-0003569:
Xinjiang Cai and David E. Clapham traced a sperm channel's evolution in this 2008 paper. CatSper channels are calcium channels found only in sperm. They drive the hyperactive swimming sperm need to reach the egg. Four subunits plus an auxiliary part form the channel complex.

Across mammals, the family showed lineage-specific gene loss. It also showed rapid evolution in the lines that kept it. Such restless history is common in reproduction genes. Sperm competition may drive that fast, uneven change. Male fertility has few drug options, so channel biology draws steady interest.
plos-pone-0003669:
Rocio G. Urdinguio, Lidia Lopez-Serra, Pilar Lopez-Nieva, and colleagues published this neurology study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Rett syndrome is a severe disorder that mainly affects girls and is tied to faults in the MECP2 gene. Mice that lack Mecp2 are a standard model of the disease.

The team searched these mice for changes in neurons that could serve as new treatment targets. Finding fresh targets matters because no cure yet exists for this disorder. Their results add candidate points where future drugs might act to ease a lifelong condition that takes skills away after early growth.
plos-pone-0003769:
Jialiang Wang, Hui Wang, Zhizhong Li, and colleagues published this brain cancer study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Malignant gliomas are among the most lethal cancers known. Their cells form a hierarchy, with cancer stem cells at the top that can regrow the tumor. The team asked what keeps those stem cells going.

They found the gene c-Myc is required for the maintenance of glioma cancer stem cells. Without Myc's support, the self-renewing core of the tumor falters. The result points to a weak spot in the hierarchy that makes gliomas so hard to kill.
plos-pone-0003869:
Ruchi Jain, Bappaditya Dey, Neeraj Dhar, and colleagues published this vaccine study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The BCG vaccine protects against tuberculosis unevenly, with efficacy from zero to eighty percent against adult disease. Better vaccine candidates are needed. One route is recombinant BCG that overproduces strong antigens of the TB bacterium.

The team built a recombinant BCG expressing the antigen Ag85C. It gave enhanced and enduring protection against tuberculosis in their tests. The stronger protection was associated with a changed cytokine profile in the lung, linking the vaccine's effect to the local immune mix. A stronger first shot could protect more of those at risk.
plos-pone-0003969:
Andrew W. Horne, John A. Phillips, Nicole Kane, and co-authors measured a receptor in ectopic pregnancy in 2008. Ectopic pregnancy happens when an embryo lodges in the Fallopian tube. It is a major cause of illness in early pregnancy. In mice, silencing the CB1 cannabinoid receptor traps embryos in the tube.

Their PLOS ONE article measured CB1 in women's Fallopian tubes and decidua. CB1 levels were lower in samples from ectopic pregnancies. That parallel with mice suggests the same system guards embryo travel in humans. The finding may help predict or prevent tubal pregnancies. The article came out in PLOS ONE, an open journal for science and health research.
plos-pone-0004069:
Thomas Fischer, Falko Nagel, Stefan Jacobs, and co-authors rechecked a cancer receptor measure in 2008. CXCR4 is a chemokine receptor that steers cell migration. It guides cancer cells toward specific sites where they seed metastases. Knowing a tumor's CXCR4 status could predict its course.

Earlier attempts to locate the receptor in tissue proved unreliable. Their PLOS ONE article validates a new rabbit antibody called UMB-2. With it, they reassessed normal and tumor tissues. A trustworthy stain is the first step toward CXCR4-guided therapy choices. The paper came out in PLOS ONE, an open journal for work in science and health.
plos-pone-0004169:
John Heidelberg and colleagues published this genomics study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Many bacteria and archaea carry CRISPR arrays, stored snippets of DNA from past invaders, together with cas genes. Together they give the microbes a form of acquired immunity against viruses.

The team read genomic data from two heat-loving Synechococcus microbes living in a microbial mat, a layered community of microbes. By comparing host CRISPR records with viral genomes from the same mat, they traced an arms race in action. The study shows germ warfare at the gene level, with hosts and viruses changing together over time.
plos-pone-0004269:
Patrick Reeves and Christopher Richards published this genetics methods paper in PLOS ONE in 2009. Spotting genetic breaks between populations is key to studies of biodiversity and evolution, and to association genetics. Small genetic breaks can hide inside one named population. The most widely used inference methods are model-based Bayesian tools that can be slow and assumption-heavy.

The authors present an approach based on principal coordinates, a statistical way to summarise genetic distances. They show it can detect subtle population structure and other genetic breaks. A lighter method for spotting fine divisions helps researchers working with large, complex samples.
plos-pone-0004369:
John Castle and colleagues published this metabolism study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Acetyl-CoA carboxylases ACC1 and ACC2 catalyse the conversion of acetyl-CoA to malonyl-CoA, controlling how fats are made and burned. They are potential targets for treating metabolic syndrome. In rodents, ACC1 is expressed in fat-making tissues and ACC2 in oxidative tissues such as muscle.

The team report that ACC2 is expressed at high levels in human white adipose tissue, contrary to the rodent pattern. They also found an isoform with a novel N-terminus. Human fat tissue breaks the rodent rule. A human-specific pattern warns against designing obesity drugs from mouse maps alone.
plos-pone-0004469:
Newborn eyes are not set at birth, and Raji Varghese, Vishnubhatla Sreenivas, Jacob Puliyel, and co-authors measured how vision at birth tracks body size and age, in PLOS ONE in 2009. It is known that babies born early tend to be shortsighted, and that this fades as the due date nears. Full-term babies are usually longsighted.

The study compared refractive status, how the eye focuses light, with birth weight and gestational age in both early and full-term babies. Such numbers help doctors know what is normal for a newborn of a given size and age. They also guide checks for babies at risk of eye problems. A clear baseline at birth makes later changes easier to spot and treat.
plos-pone-0004569:
A malaria drug is failing in northern Tanzania, and a new resistance mutation has appeared, report Samwel Gesase, Roly Gosling, Ramadhan Hashim, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. The drug pair is sulphadoxine-pyrimethamine, long used for uncomplicated malaria. It was also recommended to protect pregnant women, and was being studied for protecting infants.

The team found high resistance of Plasmodium falciparum, the deadliest malaria parasite, to the drug pair in northern Tanzania. They also report the emergence of a resistance mutation in the dhps gene at a position called codon 581. Mutations at new positions signal a drug losing ground. The findings argue for changing treatment policy before the drug fails completely in the region.
plos-pone-0004669:
John Reich, Mark Snee, and Paul Macdonald studied the fruit fly ovary for a PLOS ONE study in 2009. The ovary is a tissue where genes are often controlled after their messages are made. Past work had found many protein factors that do this control through gene screens.

More recent work found tiny RNAs called microRNAs that seem to block message use in other animals and tissues. The team asked how much this kind of block matters inside the fly ovary. Their work helps show how egg cells tune gene use without changing the genes themselves. That tuning is a core part of how eggs form and mature.
plos-pone-0004769:
Arne Egesten and colleagues showed that a strep enzyme alters both germ killing and signaling powers of human chemokines, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Chemokines are signals made by surface cells when inflamed. Some of them can also kill Streptococcus pyogenes, the bacterium that causes strep throat and deeper infections, in direct tests.

An enzyme from the bacterium cuts a wide range of chemokines. The team studied how that cutting changes both killing and receptor action. Cutting may help the bacterium evade local defense. The work shows a tug of war at infected sites. More work in larger samples can confirm how general the effect proves to be.
stowe-american-womans-home-1869:
Catharine Beecher and Harriet Beecher Stowe joined forces for The American Woman's Home in 1869. The full title calls it a guide to sound, thrifty, lovely, and Christian homes. The sisters dedicate the book to the women of America, in whose hands they say the republic's fate rests.

The introduction argues that women lack training for their duties and aims to raise home work in honor and pay. Chapters then cover house design, fresh air, cooking, cleaning, and the raising of children. Part handbook and part plea for respect, the manual treats homemaking as a skilled calling and shaped homes for years.
krylov-krilof-and-his-fables-1869:
Some two hundred verse fables by Ivan Krylov appear here in W. R. S. Ralston's English translation of 1869, Krilof and His Fables. Crows and foxes, wolves and lambs act out the vanities of Krylov's Russia in brief, quotable scenes. Russians call him their La Fontaine, and children there still learn the fables by heart.

Satirical and wise, the poems aimed at officials, flatterers, and fools of every rank. Krylov's lines entered everyday Russian speech the way proverbs do, detached from their stories. Ralston's version carried that national treasure to English readers early. The fables remain the most beloved poems in the Russian language by common consent. Their animals have been judging human beings for two centuries now.
baldwin-prehistoric-nations-1869:
John D. Baldwin argues a bold theory of the deep past in Pre-Historic Nations, from 1869. Civilization, he claims, spread from one common source in high antiquity. Ruins, languages, and customs across the world are marshaled as clues in one vast case for diffusion.

Baldwin wrote before modern archaeology settled many of these questions. His learning is real, yet his grand system now looks dated to most scholars. That is part of the book's fascination for modern readers. It preserves the great nineteenth-century debate over humanity's origins in full flight, when every new ruin seemed to rewrite the whole human story at once.
cia-0000008069:
Ghana's prospects came under CIA review in October 1961, four years after the country won independence. Kwame Nkrumah, Ghana's celebrated first leader, was tightening his grip on power. Economic strain and fading opposition raised questions in Washington about where Ghana was heading.

The paper weighs Nkrumah's rule, his ties abroad, and the chances of change from within. Ghana mattered as a model for newly free African states during the Cold War. Analysts had to judge pride, hope, and hard economics at the same time. The estimate preserves an early, clear-eyed look at postcolonial Africa's first test case.
cia-0000008669:
Italy's current situation opened the CIA's 1948 file at a tense moment in the young Cold War. Italy faced elections that April, with a strong communist party challenging Alcide De Gasperi's government. Washington feared a communist win in Western Europe's largest country.

Assessments like this one weighed parties, voters, and outside influence before the ballots were cast. Italy's choice mattered for the Marshall Plan and the shape of postwar Europe. The paper comes from the agency's first full year, yet already works at a grand scale. It shows American intelligence treating an election abroad as a strategic event.
cia-0000012269:
Readiness to devote himself to the work: that is the burden of a Russian letter translated in a CIA document from July 1960. The translation belongs to the Penkovsky file, and its words carry a would-be spy's pledge. Oleg Penkovsky was then offering himself to the West, asking to be taken on as a source inside Soviet intelligence.

The document preserves the translated text and its handling marks. Pledges like this one opened the most valuable Western penetration of the Soviet military. For readers, the page holds the operation's human beginning: one officer's decision, rendered into English.
cia-0000013869: Two American prisoners were seen near Son Tay City, and a CIA note dated July 4, 1967, reports the sighting. Son Tay sits in Ha Tay Province, west of Hanoi. A sighting near a known prison area drew close attention in Washington. Notes of this kind helped build the picture of where the camp system held its men.
cia-0000014769: Communist activities in Argentina fill a CIA file dated March 3, 1953. The file names the Partido Comunista de la Argentina, the country's Communist Party, and a man cut short as Juan in the title. Party watching in Latin America was steady work for U.S. stations. The file adds one month of that watch to the record.
cia-0000015369: A meeting of the Upper Atmosphere Rocket Research Panel fills a CIA file dated August 4, 1954. Rocket men met to plan study of the high sky in those years. Their work touched the same heights where strange objects were claimed. The file places the saucer era beside the earnest science of the rocket age.
cia-0000015469: Sightings over Spain and Africa from July to October fill a CIA record dated in 1952. The title gives a four month span, longer than most single sighting notes. It also names Africa, not Portugal, whatever older summaries say. A seasonal bundle like this let analysts scan a whole region's reports at once and look for patterns across the busy summer and fall.
cia-0000022669: The pacification effort in Vietnam, with information on the Phoenix Program and Viet Cong infrastructure, fills a CIA record dated in 1969. Pacification meant winning villages away from the Viet Cong by aid, guard work, and pressure. The Phoenix Program targeted the Viet Cong's shadow leadership and drew lasting dispute. The record joins a broad campaign survey to its most debated part.
cia-0000037169:
Autopsies were allegedly performed on the bodies of American pilots at a place in Quang Ninh province, a CIA record dated October 5, 1968 states. The claim is among the grimmest in the wartime prisoner files. Quang Ninh lies in the far northeast of North Vietnam, near the Chinese border.

The record preserves the allegation as it was reported during the war itself. Charges of this kind fed anger in the United States and hardened public feeling. For later readers, the file shows the darkest edge of the prisoner story, where rumor and fact were painfully hard to separate from each other.
cia-0000049069: Recommendations by the Salvadoran army's political commission on points raised in a meeting fill a CIA item from 1983. Armies at war keep political staffs to watch the civilian game, and this commission spoke for the institution. Its advice, preserved here, shows soldiers weighing speeches and parties as carefully as battles.
cia-0000049269: A session of the PCC on El Salvador in 1991 is preserved in a CIA item, kept with the Truth Commission records. The Policy Coordinating Committee was where the government's agencies hammered out one line on a country. Meeting on El Salvador in 1991 meant planning for a war everyone could see ending.
cia-0000049369: Leftist Death Squads is the blunt title of declassified CIA document 0000049369, dated May 5, 1985. Noted for the Truth Commission, the item directs attention to death squads on the left in the Salvadoran conflict. Readers get a short declassified record whose heading names its subject without qualification, preserved among the agency's many short Salvadoran items.
cia-0000098269: Increasing civil unrest in Kwangsi, Hupeh, Peking, Fukien and Yunnan is reported in declassified CIA document 0000098269, dated June 6, 1968. Five places are named in one heading, a wider sweep than most. Readers get a short multi-place unrest account from China, its long place list the record's most distinctive feature. The heading and date are the firm facts the catalog gives.

Jonathan Scholz and colleagues showed distinct regions of right temporo parietal junction are selective for theory of mind and attention, in PLOS ONE in 2009. In fMRI studies, a cortical region in right temporo parietal junction is recruited when participants read stories about thoughts. Lesion and imaging studies also suggest a nearby region assists exogenous attention, raising the question whether one area serves both social cognition and attention reorienting.

Neighboring subregions separate the two functions cleanly. Overlap in earlier scans reflected coarse resolution. Social and attention networks remain distinct. Autism and neglect research benefit. Taken together, the findings mark a useful step for research in this area.
plos-pone-0005469:
Camilla Rathcke and colleagues studied a gene linked to diabetes in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. The gene CHI3L1 makes a protein called YKL-40, which rises with inflammation in the body. People with type 2 diabetes tend to have more of it in their blood, in step with how resistant they are to insulin.

The team checked whether common forms of the gene track with diabetes or with related traits such as weight and blood sugar. Testing the gene itself helps show whether YKL-40 is a cause of disease or just a sign that disease is present.
plos-pone-0005569:
Monika Zochowska and co-authors tested a virus shell as a drug carrier in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Bleomycin is a drug used against several cancers. Its use is limited because it can scar the lungs, an effect that can be fatal in a few patients.

The team loaded the drug into hollow protein shells built by a virus, shaped like a twelve-sided ball. Carrying the drug inside a shell could steer it toward tumours and away from the lungs. Early work like this tests whether such carriers are safe and practical.
plos-pone-0005669:
Gwen Robbins and co-authors reported in 2009 on a skeleton from ancient India that shows signs of leprosy. The bones date to about 2000 B.C., making them among the oldest direct proof of the disease. Leprosy is a long-lasting infection that still affects many thousands of people each year.

The team reads the damage in the bones against what is known about how and when leprosy spread. Genes from the modern germ point to a long shared past with humans, but hard dates have been scarce. A dated case from India helps pin down where the disease was, and when, early in its history.
plos-pone-0005769:
Teruhisa Hirai and Sriram Subramaniam compared two ways of picturing a light-driven protein in 2009. Bacteriorhodopsin pumps protons across a membrane when light hits it, changing shape as it works. Over thirty structure sets, from X-ray and electron methods, claim to show its steps.

The pair checked where the two methods agree on the protein's movements, and where they clash. Clash points may be artifacts of how crystals were made or frozen. Sorting real motion from artifact matters for all membrane protein work. Bacteriorhodopsin is the test case for methods used across drug target research.
plos-pone-0005869:
Colleen Novak and co-authors argued in 2009 that stamina, not body size, sets how much an animal moves each day. Some people stay lean despite pressure to gain weight, and lean people tend to be more active. Where that extra activity comes from was unknown.

In lean and obesity-resistant models, leanness could not be explained by eating less for their weight. Instead, a muscle enzyme, PEPCK, tracked with higher endurance and spontaneous activity. Muscles built for stamina may drive a generally restless, lean life. The finding reframes leanness as partly a muscle trait, not only an appetite trait.
plos-pone-0006469:
Louisa Hooven and co-authors asked whether the time of day changes pesticide effects, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Circadian clocks drive daily rhythms in body and molecular processes. Genes that break down foreign chemicals, called xenobiotic metabolizing genes, may rise and fall with those rhythms. Such rhythms could change the outcome of chemical exposure at different hours.

The team examined responses to pesticides across the daily cycle. Their title poses the question of whether the clock makes the poison. If timing matters, safety tests done at one hour may mislead. Farmers, workers, and regulators may need to think about when exposure happens, not just how much.
plos-pone-0006569:
Tomasz Leski and co-authors validated a chip for detecting biothreat agents in PLOS ONE in 2009. Rapid and effective detection of emerging microbiological threats and potential biowarfare agents is very challenging with traditional culture-based methods. Culture takes days and misses organisms that grow poorly. The team tested a high density resequencing microarray for broad range detection.

Resequencing chips read the DNA of many pathogens at once. Validation shows how accurate and sensitive the chip is across agents. A broad, fast detector serves both public health and biodefense. The study is a benchmark for replacing slow culture with DNA-based screening.
plos-pone-0009469:
Cheryl Carling and colleagues tested how wording shapes a health choice in PLOS ONE in 2010. Blood pressure drugs cut the risk of heart attacks and strokes. The same benefit can be stated in more than one way. The team ran an online trial with people who had just learned they had high blood pressure. Each person saw one of three ways of framing the benefit.

Which framing people saw changed how many chose to start the drug. The trial shows that words at the point of prescribing carry real weight. Doctors can use the results to present benefits in a fair, clear way. Good wording may help more patients take a drug that can save their lives.
plos-pone-0009569:
Jason Bragg, Stephanie Dutkiewicz, and Oliver Jahn modeled ocean microbes in PLOS ONE in 2010. Phytoplankton are tiny drifting plants that base the ocean food web. New tools had revealed far more kinds of them than anyone expected. Making sense of that flood of data is hard. The team built a model of which forces shape these microbes across the world ocean.

Their model weighs forces such as nutrient supply, light, and grazing in each region. It shows how the balance of forces differs from sea to sea. That helps explain why the same group thrives in one place and not another. The work brings order to a fast growing picture of ocean life.
plos-pone-0009669:
Ines Samengo and Marcelo Montemurro modeled a code change in nerve cells in PLOS ONE in 2010. Neurons can fire in bursts, and the timing within a burst carries information. That timing is called phase information. Downstream cells, though, may simply count spikes. The team asked how bursting neurons convert phase information into a spike count code. Their model follows that translation step by step.

The conversion shows how the brain can repack the same message in a new format. A count code is simpler for some readers, while timing is richer. Knowing the translation helps decode real recordings from the brain. It may also inspire computing designs that switch codes as neurons do.
plos-pone-0010469:
Irina Lyadova and colleagues followed tuberculosis in mice to see how lung inflammation tracks with disease course for PLOS ONE in 2010. TB infection ends many ways, from quiet containment to rapid, fatal illness. What decides the path in otherwise healthy hosts was unclear. The team infected mice and watched their lungs over time. They measured inflammation and the cells gathering there.

As disease advanced, inflammation grew intense rather than protective. A particular cell type, marked Gr-1 dim, piled up in the lungs. Heavy inflammation may itself drive damage in progressing TB. That flips a simple view where more immune response is always better. The study helps explain why some hosts lose control of the infection.
plos-pone-0010569:
Philippe Halfon and colleagues asked whether semen can still carry HIV when blood treatment works well in PLOS ONE in 2010. Effective therapy can drive blood virus to undetectable levels. Whether the male genital tract matches that clearance was uncertain. The team studied men on therapy in France over several years. They tested semen for HIV despite good blood control.

Finding virus in semen would mean a residual transmission risk remains. Male-to-female transmission risk per act is low but not zero. The study's answer informs counseling for couples where one partner has HIV. It also probes the idea of body compartments where drugs reach poorly. Residual risk questions are central to treatment-as-prevention policy.
plos-pone-0010669:
Sibo Tian, Robert Haney, and Martin Feder traced the history of heat-shock gene switches in fruit flies, in PLOS ONE in 2010. When cells overheat, heat-shock genes switch on within minutes. Short DNA motifs in front of each gene, called heat-shock elements, trigger that response.

Comparing species on the fly family tree cleaned up a confused picture. Some motif arrangements were old, while others arose recently in single lineages. Family history, not guesswork, separated true shared patterns from look-alikes. The cleaned history helps explain how a life-saving stress response stays fast while still evolving.
plos-pone-0010869:
Cedar Chittenden, Michael Melnychuk, David Welch and co-authors published this salmon study in PLOS ONE in 2010. A coho salmon population in British Columbia's Thompson River is endangered, and managers did not know where its young fish were dying. The team fitted juvenile salmon, called smolts, with tiny acoustic tags and followed them downstream.

Tracked over three years, the smolts took between ten and sixteen days to reach the lower Fraser River, but very few were ever detected on ocean tracking arrays. Freshwater survival was near zero in the first year and rose sharply by the third. Return rates of adults followed the same pattern. Chittenden and colleagues conclude that many young fish die before ever reaching the sea, shifting conservation focus onto the river itself.
plos-pone-0010969:
Gabriele Möller, Bettina Husen, Dorota Kowalik and co-authors published this enzyme study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Some breast cancers and endometriosis feed on estrogen made locally by an enzyme called 17beta-HSD1, and blocking it is a promising treatment idea. The team tested new blocker candidates built on a hormone scaffold, checking carefully what else they might hit.

They measured the compounds against five related human enzymes and against the target enzyme from marmoset, pig, mouse, and rat, the species used in drug screening. Susceptibility differed profoundly: rodent versions of the enzyme were much less sensitive to the blockers than the human one. Möller and colleagues warn that a candidate can look weak in a mouse and strong in a person, or the reverse, distorting preclinical decisions.
plos-pone-0011069:
Ann Moore, Mary Biggs, Amy Matteini and co-authors published this aging study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Frailty, the syndrome of weakness, slowness, and shrinking that leaves older adults vulnerable, has been linked to failing mitochondria, the cell's power plants. The authors tested whether inherited variation in mitochondrial DNA helps decide who becomes frail.

Drawing on a long-running population study of older Americans, they compared mitochondrial variants between frail and non-frail participants and explored links to muscle strength. Frailty was scored from five standard indicators at the study's baseline examinations. Moore and colleagues bring mitochondrial genetics into the frailty question. That matters for a clear reason. A genetic link would point to energy use in cells as a lever for prevention. Exercise, or drugs that support mitochondria, could pull that lever.
plos-pone-0011169:
Hlevnjak, Zitkovic and Zagrovic proposed a binding rule in PLOS ONE in 2010. For two proteins to form a working pair inside a cell, many traits must match. The authors argued that matching love of water, called hydrophilicity, may be a basic first requirement for pairing.

If partner proteins share similar water affinity, they may meet and stick more readily in the watery cell interior. A simple rule like this could help predict which proteins work together. Such predictions speed the mapping of cell networks, which is slow to test one pair at a time. The idea now invites tests in real protein data.
plos-pone-0011269:
Gawecka, Griffiths, Ek-Rylander and colleagues traced melanoma movement in PLOS ONE in 2010. For skin cancer to spread, its cells must grip surfaces and crawl. The team studied a small switch protein and its handshake with a scaffolding protein that shapes the cell's inner frame.

That interaction regulated how melanoma cells migrate. A defined motility circuit gives drug designers specific points to jam. Stopping crawl would not kill the first tumor, but could halt the spread that makes melanoma lethal. The study adds molecular detail to the search for anti metastasis drugs.
plos-pone-0011369:
Rudy Jonker and co-authors asked in 2010 why barnacle geese had shifted the timing of their spring migration. The geese travel from wintering grounds to Arctic breeding sites, and their departure and stopover dates had moved over recent years. Food and weather were the usual suspects, but the team tested another pressure: the danger from predators along the route.

Their analysis found that predation risk fits the new timing well, as if geese adjust travel to dodge the most dangerous places and moments. Safer timing can mean arriving when predators are scarce, even at some cost to feeding. The result broadens how migration change is explained. Climate is not the only moving force; a shifting map of danger may redraw flyways just as strongly.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1269:
The British Chiefs of Staff issued this memorandum on 20 July 1945. It follows their paper of two days before in the volume's run. The British staff kept its own steady pace of advice as the first week closed.

Each note took up the military questions as London's chiefs saw them: forces, fronts, and the means to hold what the talks might win. This one continues that series. Together the British memoranda form a staff diary of the summit from the soldiers' side. They let readers trace how the military view held or shifted as the bargaining moved.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1369:
The Soviet delegation presented another proposal at Potsdam on 22 July 1945, one of a run of Soviet papers in the volume's last section. Each proposal fixed Moscow's wording on a point under dispute. It is printed in volume two of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record of American diplomacy at Potsdam.

Reading the Soviet papers in order shows a method: state a claim in full, then bargain down only as far as needed. This proposal came as the conference moved past first speeches into hard drafting. For students of the talks, the value lies in contrast. Readers can set what the Soviet side tabled beside what all three leaders signed at the end. The gap between those texts is the story of Potsdam in brief.
frus-1945-50-intel-d69:
Harold Smith, the budget director, set down a memorandum on his own part in the settlement on 9 January 1946. Smith rarely wrote without a purpose, and self-recording was among his habits. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

Memoranda written for the file by the men who shaped events are gifts to readers, when read with care. Smith knew his bureau's plan had largely won, and his paper helps explain how. Set beside the secretaries' joint letter of the same week, it shows the two tracks of the settlement. The departments agreeing in public, the budget director noting in private how the agreement was built. The volume's balance of open and office papers is nowhere better shown.
frus-1945-50-intel-d169:
The meeting named in the title took place on 25 September 1946, and these minutes are its formal record. The State Department prints it as document 169 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. The National Intelligence Authority, set up in January 1946, oversaw the Director of Central Intelligence and his Central Intelligence Group.

Minutes are the formal record of a meeting: who sat in, what was put on the table, and what the group agreed to do. They rarely give long speeches, but they fix the choices that later memos then carry out. For a reader of the period, the piece fills one link in the chain between the war's end and the settled Cold War system.
frus-1945-50-intel-d269: Dated 4 May 1948, "Policy Planning Staff Memorandum" comes from the top level of the government. Readers meet it as document 269 of the Foreign Relations series volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. It was the CIA's first full year, and the Council was setting the rules for both open analysis and secret work. Inside the government, memos were how business got done between meetings.
frus-1945-50-intel-d369:
A memorandum from the Assistant Director for Reports and Estimates (Babbitt) reached Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter on 17 February 1949. The State Department prints it as document 369 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. While the survey team asked its questions, the CIA's covert arm was growing fast under Frank Wisner.

Such notes moved business along: they told a busy reader what had happened, what it meant, and what should come next. The points are stated once and left to stand; the file around it holds the answer they drew. Its worth lies in the trail it leaves: a dated, signed step in the long build-up of the CIA and the Council.
frus-1861-d69:
One of three letters dated 17 August 1861 went from William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams. The letter is document 69 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

The date 17 August opens a cluster of three Seward letters to London in one day. Each took up a point of its own, from notes to claims. Together they show the range of business that crossed the Secretary's desk in the war's first summer. The cluster form of 17 August shows in the printed file as three short papers in a row. Three short papers in a row show the file at its most clerk neat that summer.
frus-1861-d169:
Carl Schurz wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 15 July 1861. The dispatch is document 169 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Schurz wrote with the flair of the journalist he had been. His Madrid reports mixed court fact with sharp judgment of men. This July letter shows the new minister finding his feet at a proud, formal court in wartime. His flair for phrase later made his memoirs a classic of the German American story. A classic memoir grew from the same pen that penned these wartime pages. The same pen later wrote a classic memoir.
frus-1861-d269:
By the date of 23 November 1861, Seward had new word ready for James Shepherd Pike, the American minister to the Netherlands. Congress received it as Document 269 in the papers printed with the President's message that year. The letter comes from the autumn of the war's first year, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1862-d69:
Home in Washington, Seward read a fresh report from Charles Francis Adams, dated 22 May 1862. Congress received it as Document 69 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. By then, in the spring of 1862, a year into the war, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

Readers get the field report side of the exchange, sent home for Seward to weigh and answer. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1862-d169:
Printed as Document 169, the third Seward dispatch of 25 October 1862 went from Washington to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. Together the three letters show one day's full output from the Secretary of State's desk to his British post.

Short letters, sent often, were how a government without cables ran an embassy in wartime. Each one might carry a single order or a single piece of news. A lone dispatch like this one grows in value when read in its cluster. Set in that stream, it helped keep London and Washington in step. Adams reported home at least once a week, and oftener when the news was hot.
frus-1862-d269:
On 22 April 1862 William L. Dayton sent Secretary of State William H. Seward a report printed as Document 269 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It was one of two Paris papers under that date, the other being a Seward dispatch.

Late April brought the Union flag back over New Orleans, a loss the South felt in every European counting house. Cotton, credit, and sympathy all shifted with such news. Dayton's report from Paris that week belongs to the record of how France absorbed the blow to the Confederate cause it was tempted to aid.
