Policy at Napoleon III's court was made in private, so an envoy's ear mattered as much as his pen.
frus-1862-d369: A translated paper dated 31 July 1862 stands as Document 369 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Filed in the French section after the Mercier letters. The heading marks it only as a translation, giving no author or reader. So the entry rests on its date, its form, and its place among the French papers of that summer.
frus-1862-d469:
George Perkins Marsh wrote from Turin to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 4 April 1862. His dispatch is Document 469 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, laid before Congress with the annual message.

Spring 1862 found Italy watching France closely, since French troops still guarded the pope in Rome and French ambition was moving in Mexico. Marsh's reports linked those Italian concerns to the American war, which shared the same French question. From Turin he could also report the new kingdom's steady sympathy for the Union. The letter is part of the volume's Italian file, where diplomacy ran on shared national hopes rather than on fear or bargaining.
frus-1862-d569:
Henry Shelton Sanford sent this report from Brussels to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 26 September 1862. It is Document 569 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed with the annual message.

Sanford wrote four days after Lincoln's emancipation order was issued, though the news was still crossing the Atlantic. His report covered the Brussels scene as it stood: the court's connections, the press, and the war's standing in Belgian opinion. Within days he would have the emancipation news to work with, and few ministers used it more eagerly. The letter catches the Belgian file at the hinge of the autumn. The war's new moral shape had not yet reached Europe. When it did, it changed Sanford's brief for the better.
frus-1862-d669:
On 24 December 1861, Anson Burlingame wrote from China to Secretary of State William H. Seward. Burlingame was the American minister there, a former congressman turned envoy. His letter is document 669 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862.

A Christmas Eve date on a letter from the far side of the world hints at the pace of the post. Mail from China took months to reach Washington, so envoys wrote often and covered much ground in each sheet. Burlingame's dispatch is part of that steady flow, the raw stuff from which the State Department built its view of China in the war years.
frus-1863p1-d69:
William H. Seward sent this letter to Charles Francis Adams on 2 February 1863. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 69 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863, opening Seward's February mail in the file.

February brought no rest to the London brief. The South's agents still worked for ships and friends in Britain, and the Union's claims still needed pressing. Seward's letters kept Adams supplied with the government's views and the facts from home. This one opens a run of February sheets that runs thick in the volume, proof of how much of the war was fought with pens.
frus-1863p1-d169:
Charles Francis Adams closed a three-letter day with this dispatch of 24 April 1863 to Secretary of State William H. Seward. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 169 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

The last of Adams's three sheets wound up the legation's work for a peak day in the file. His spring letters, read whole, are the story of the Union's cause in Britain told by its keeper. This one ends the 24 April set. It stands in the record as a working piece of the watch that kept Britain's fleet and yards from the South.
frus-1863p1-d269: Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, sent this report to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 21 August 1863. It is document 269 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, part of the London correspondence on Britain and the Civil War. Letters on this route carried Adams's reading of British policy while Washington worked to keep Britain from backing the Confederacy.
frus-1863p1-d369:
A formal note dated 26 January 1863 passed from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, in Washington. It stands as document 369 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress.

British subjects caught up in the war, as sailors, traders, or prisoners, gave London steady grounds for protest. Seward's notes answered those complaints one case at a time. It is a small piece of a huge correspondence, but the whole picture only emerges from pieces like this one.
frus-1863p1-d469:
A 20 April 1863 dispatch from Secretary of State William H. Seward reached Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington. Behind the formal phrases stood a live question: would Britain stay neutral, or step into the American war? At the time, the Union government was fighting the Confederacy at home and working to keep foreign powers neutral.

The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them. The stakes behind this routine mail were high. If Britain had backed the Confederacy, the war could have changed course, so each note helped hold the line of British neutrality. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1863p1-d569:
William H. Seward, Secretary of State received a letter dated 17 June 1863 from Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight.

The formal tone can hide the tension, but the pace gives it away. Notes this frequent mean both capitals were watching each other closely. Much of the mail between the two offices turned on ships: the Union blockade, seized cargoes, and Confederate agents buying vessels in British ports. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
frus-1863p1-d669:
Among the day's business on 19 November 1863 was a letter from Charles Francis Adams to William H. Seward. Adams was the American minister in London, and Seward was Secretary of State in Washington. Mail between London and Washington crossed the Atlantic by steamer, so each reply took weeks to complete the round trip. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight.

From the London end, the work was pressure and reporting. Adams pushed the British government on Confederate shipbuilding and sent home his reading of British politics and opinion. Read in sequence, the London letters show how close the two countries came to open conflict, and how both sides kept stepping back. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.
plos-pbio-0000069:
Unnur Styrkarsdottir, Jean-Baptiste Cazier, Augustine Kong, and others mapped an osteoporosis risk region in PLOS Biology in 2003. Their search ties weak bones to chromosome 20 and to BMP2, a gene known for helping bone form. Osteoporosis thins bone and raises the risk of breaks in older people.

The team used family data to find where the risk sits in the genome, then narrowed it to a gene that fits the biology. That link matters because bone density runs in families, yet the genes behind it were mostly unknown. Naming a region and a likely gene gives drug and diagnosis work a place to start. It also helps explain why some people lose bone faster than others.
plos-pbio-0020069:
Martin Wu, Ling V. Sun, Jessica Vamathevan, and a big team sequenced a parasite genome for PLOS Biology in 2004. Wolbachia pipientis wMel lives inside fruit fly cells and bends the fly's reproduction to spread itself. Its whole genome runs to about 1.27 million DNA letters.

For a free-living bacterium that genome is small and stripped down. Yet it is packed with mobile DNA elements that copy and move within the genome, an odd trait for so compact a genome. The full sequence lets researchers compare Wolbachia strains and track how it manipulates hosts. That knowledge may aid pest control, since Wolbachia infects many insect species of concern.
plos-pbio-0020369:
Olaf Sporns and Rolf Kötter analyzed patterns in brain wiring in PLOS Biology in 2004. Brain networks can be read as maps of nodes and links. Small recurring link patterns, called motifs, appear more often than chance would suggest, much as common words recur in a language.

The authors catalogued motifs in brain maps from several species and compared them with random networks. Certain motifs stood out, hinting at design rules for how brains are wired. Motif counts give a compact way to compare healthy and disordered brains, or brains across species. The paper helped bring network math into neuroscience, where it now shapes how brain maps are read.
plos-pone-0000069:
Lester M. Shulman, Yossi Manor, Danit Sofer, and a large team searched sewage for poliovirus in PLOS ONE in 2006. In places where most people are vaccinated, the live polio vaccine itself can, on rare occasions, change back toward a harmful form. Those vaccine-derived viruses can pass through the gut and out into sewage.

Finding them in sewage is an early warning that they are circulating. The team reports such neurovirulent strains in a highly immune population, where few would expect them. Sewage testing thus acts as a silent sentinel for polio control. It can spot risk before any child falls ill, which is exactly what the endgame of polio eradication needs.
plos-pone-0000169:
Roderick Nigel Finn and Børge A. Kristoffersen published this evolution paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Vitellogenin is the protein that stocks fish eggs with yolk. The authors examine how this gene was duplicated in vertebrates, testing the so-called 3R hypothesis of genome doublings. They link the copies to the floating pelagic egg and to the great spread of teleost fishes in the oceans.

Teleosts make up most fish species alive today, so their egg strategy matters at scale. The authors connect gene duplication timing to the rise of the buoyant ocean egg. The paper ties a DNA-level event to one of the biggest radiations in vertebrate history.
plos-pone-0000269:
Doris Estrugo, Alexander Fischer, Franziska Hess, and colleagues published this leukemia study in PLOS ONE in 2007. Integrins are the anchors cells use to grip their surroundings, and beta1 integrins sit on leukemia cells. The authors report that when these anchors are bound to their ligands, they inhibit procaspase-8, a starter protein of cell death. In doing so they mediate resistance to drugs and radiation that depends on cell adhesion.

Leukemia cells hiding in the bone marrow can survive chemotherapy by gripping their niche. This paper names the molecular brake that grip applies to the death machinery. Blocking that protective signal could make standard treatments work on cells that currently outlast them.
plos-pone-0000369:
Daryl Wile and Evan Balaban explored how the brain hears pitch, in a paper published in PLOS ONE in 2007. When people hear a musical note, they sense one whole pitch even when the sound is built from many parts. The authors looked for a brain signal that matches that whole-note sense of pitch.

Their study reports an auditory neural correlate, a pattern of brain activity that tracks pitch as a single quality rather than piece by piece. Work of this kind helps explain how the hearing system builds a simple sensation out of complex sound. It also bears on how people perceive music and speech, where pitch carries much of the meaning.
plos-pone-0000469:
Claude Sadis and colleagues found a protective side to nicotine in kidney injury, reporting in PLOS ONE in 2007. The injury model is ischemia/reperfusion, where blood flow to the kidney stops and then returns, paradoxically causing extra damage through inflammation. The team showed nicotine protects the kidney from this injury through the cholinergic anti-inflammatory pathway.

That pathway is a nerve-based brake on inflammation, triggered through the same receptors nicotine acts on. The finding does not make smoking safe; it isolates one drug-like action worth copying without tobacco. Separating nicotine's anti-inflammatory effect from its harms is the kind of lead that can seed new medicines for transplant and shock patients.
plos-pone-0000569:
David Liska and colleagues compared how body fat is distributed among obese teenagers of different backgrounds, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The team measured interethnic differences in fat partitioning in obese adolescents. They looked at muscle, liver, and abdominal fat. Where fat is stored matters as much as how much there is.

Fat in the liver and deep abdomen drives diabetes and heart risk far more than fat under the skin. If ethnic groups partition fat differently at the same weight, risk screening by weight alone will misjudge many teens. Studies like this argue for measuring the dangerous depots directly in high-risk youth.
plos-pone-0000669:
Gilles Mirambeau, Sébastien Lyonnais, Dominique Coulaud and co-authors watched two HIV enzymes shape the virus's inner shell, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The HIV-1 nucleocapsid forms as the virus matures, a process directed by the viral protease. After infection, reverse transcriptase copies the viral genome, and the nucleocapsid transforms into pre-integration complexes in the cell's cytoplasm.

Using transmission electron microscopy in detail, the team examined the nucleocapsid's architecture. Their title states that protease and reverse transcriptase together control that structure. Both enzymes are already drug targets. Showing they also act as architects adds a new way to think about blocking the virus.
plos-pone-0000769:
Joern Kamradt, Volker Jung, Kerstin Wahrheit and colleagues scanned prostate cancer cell lines for newly amplified genome regions, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Their purpose was to prove a longmer oligonucleotide microarray platform can profile gene copy number alterations. Amplicons are stretches of DNA copied many times in cancer cells. A genome-wide screen of such changes can quickly indicate novel candidate genes.

Candidates flagged this way may play a role in carcinogenesis, the making of cancer. Comprehensive profiling replaces one-gene-at-a-time searching with a single sweep. Each new amplicon is a lead: somewhere inside it may sit a gene whose extra copies drive tumor growth, and which drugs could target.
plos-pone-0000869:
Britta Eickholt, Aminul Ahmed, Meirion Davies and co-authors studied a single enzyme form called p110 delta in nerve growth, for PLOS ONE in 2007. The enzyme belongs to the PI 3-kinase family, which has eight forms whose roles in the nervous system were unclear. The p110 delta form was mostly known from white blood cells.

The team asked what this form does in sensory neurons, the cells that carry signals from skin and muscle. They focused on how axons, the long fibers of nerve cells, grow and regrow after damage. Knowing which enzyme form drives regrowth could guide later work on nerve repair.
plos-pone-0000969:
Eleonora Castelletti, Sergio Lo Caputo, Louise Kuhn and colleagues studied a mucosal signal chemical in HIV infection, in PLOS ONE in 2007. The chemical, CCL28 or MEC, draws antibody making cells into moist body linings. Those cells release IgA, the antibody that guards mucosal surfaces.

HIV specific IgA shows up both in infected people and in some exposed people who stay uninfected. The team analyzed the CCL28 circuit across infected, exposed and unexposed groups. Mucosal defense is where HIV usually enters, so its local signals matter. Work of this kind may help explain why a few exposed people resist infection.
plos-pone-0001069:
Sacha Genovesi, Liviana Leita, Paolo Sequi and colleagues directly detected prions bound in soil, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Scrapie in sheep and chronic wasting disease in deer are contagious prion diseases. Spread through the environment seems important in keeping these epidemics going, with contaminated ground as a reservoir.

Detecting prions in soil, rather than inferring them from sick animals, was the missing step. The team present a direct detection method for soil bound prions. Land where deer or sheep gather could then be tested before animals are moved there. Environmental control of prion disease depends on exactly this kind of tool.
plos-pone-0001169:
Building a brain means first making many progenitor cells, then having them stop dividing and become neurons. Barbara Hämmerle and Francisco Tejedor describe a new role for the Delta-Notch signaling system in that switch, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The transition from proliferation to neurogenesis is a crucial step in development.

The authors report a novel function of Delta-Notch signaling that mediates this transition in neural progenitor cells. A complete account of neurogenesis needs the molecular processes that govern each such step. Their finding adds a control point that other researchers can probe when development goes wrong.
plos-pone-0001269:
Hutchinson-Gilford progeria is a rare disorder of accelerated aging, caused in most cases by a specific mutation in the LMNA gene. Dayle McClintock and colleagues report that the mutant protein appears in ordinary aging skin too, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. Progeria patients age fast and often die early, frequently from stroke or heart disease.

The authors show that the mutant form of lamin A acts as a biomarker of cellular aging in human skin, detectable beyond the disease itself. In other words, the progeria mechanism leaves traces in normal aging. That widens the relevance of studying this rare disease.
plos-pone-0001369:
Christopher Kanakry and co-authors published a 2007 PLOS ONE study on a growth factor called neuregulin-1. The gene for this factor has been linked to a higher risk of a severe mental illness. The same factor also plays a part in how the brain grows and how cancer spreads through the body.

Using blood cells grown in the lab, the team traced how the factor helps cells stick to each other. They found a chain of signals inside the cell that drives this effect. The findings tie one gene to both brain growth and cancer spread. That link may guide new work on both fields.
plos-pone-0001469:
Jun Cui and colleagues wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE model of the switch that tells a cell to die. A family of proteins acts as a checkpoint for this death program, called apoptosis. How its parts interact was still in dispute. The team's past models had backed one account of the switch over others.

Here they show the switch holds two self boosting loops that can lock it in two states. Such a lock makes cell death a firm, one way choice once it flips. A clear model helps labs test drugs that flip the switch in cancer. It also explains why half measures tend to fail in this system.
plos-pone-0001569:
Yanjun Jiang, Dongsheng Xu, and Yong Zhao published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on two cancer viruses in one tumor type. Both viruses, tied to Kaposi's sarcoma and to mono, belong to one virus family. Most cases of a rare AIDS linked lymphoma carry both. Each virus can wake and copy itself via a starter protein.

The team show the two starters hold each other back when both viruses share a cell. That mutual brake may keep both viruses quiet in the tumor. It is a neat case of rivals checking each other. It also shapes how drugs that wake one virus might act on the pair.
plos-pone-0001669:
Laurent Gillet, Susanna Colaco, and Philip G. Stevenson studied how a mouse herpesvirus first grabs hold of cells, in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The first contact a virus makes largely decides which cells it can infect. Murid herpesvirus-4 depends heavily on glycosaminoglycans, long sugar chains on cell surfaces, for binding.

That dependence pointed to one of the virus's own surface glycoproteins as the sugar-binding part. The authors tested the gH and gL protein pair and report that this complex binds glycosaminoglycans. The full text gives the binding assays and the mutants they used to confirm the contact. A virus's first grip on a cell is a natural drug and vaccine target, since blocking it can stop infection before it starts.
plos-pone-0001769:
Sylvane Desrivières, Kristina Krause, Anne Dyer, and their co-authors linked a signaling gene to teenage drinking behavior in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The PI3K pathway usually regulates cell growth and survival. Growing evidence tied it to behavioral responses to addictive drugs, which made its genes candidates for addiction risk.

The team reports that sequence variation in the PI3K p85 alpha gene associates with alcohol risk drinking behavior in adolescents. The full text gives the teen sample and the variant statistics. A gene in a drug-response pathway showing up in teenage drinking supports the view that addiction risk is partly hard-wired. That could one day guide early prevention for high-risk youth.
plos-pone-0001869:
Hiroshi Ageta and co-authors published a brain study in PLOS ONE in 2008 on activin, a hormone that helps cells grow and change type. Activin was already known to shield brain cells from harm when blood flow fails. The team asked what else activin does inside the brain. They focused on mood, and on the growth of new brain cells in adult animals.

The authors report that activin in the brain shapes acts linked to fear and stress. It also shapes adult neurogenesis, the birth of new neurons in grown animals. Readers get a clear case that a growth hormone can sway both behavior and brain repair. That link matters for work on mood disorders and on how the adult brain renews itself.
plos-pone-0001969:
Michael Forbes and co-authors compared ear infection strains of a common bacterium in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The bacterium, Streptococcus pneumoniae, causes both local ills, such as ear infection, and body-wide disease. How much of that variety comes from the strain's genes, its serotype, or the host's response was not fully clear.

The team used a chinchilla model of otitis media, infection of the middle ear, to score each strain's virulence under the same host conditions. Holding the host fixed lets strain traits stand out. Such scores help predict which strains cause the worst disease, and which a vaccine must cover.
plos-pone-0002069:
Paloma Alonso-Magdalena and co-authors studied how estrogen shapes insulin stores in the pancreas, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Pancreatic beta cells make and release insulin, the main hormone that keeps blood sugar in balance. Estrogen receptors, in two forms called alpha and beta, play a part in glucose control, yet their role inside beta cells was still grey.

As the title states, the team report that the alpha form, ER alpha, regulates how much insulin the pancreas holds. A hormone better known for reproduction thus also tunes the insulin supply. That link may help explain sex gaps in diabetes risk.
plos-pone-0002169:
Omar Salim, Ian Clarke, and Paul Lambden examined the front end of the genome of a cattle virus, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Jena virus is a bovine norovirus that causes gut disease in cattle. It serves as a workable model for the noroviruses that infect the gut of people, which are hard to study directly.

The virus carries a single strand of RNA with sections that code first for building proteins, then for its shell. The team analyzed the 5 prime end of that genome to see how its parts are arranged and controlled. Details at this level guide work on how noroviruses copy themselves.
plos-pone-0002269:
Mahomed Patel and co-authors built a framework for judging how ready family doctors are for a flu pandemic. Their paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Primary care, and general practice above all, will stand at the frontline when pandemic influenza hits. Yet no framework existed to guide systematic planning for that task or to compare the plans countries had drawn up.

The authors aimed to create such a framework and to test it against plans from five countries. A common yardstick lets health systems spot the gaps in their own plans before a crisis exposes them. General practice is where most patients will first turn.
plos-pone-0002369:
Liao and co-authors published a research article in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Anne P. Liao, Elaine O. Petrof, Sumalatha Kuppireddi, among others. Its subject is salmonella Type III Effector AvrA Stabilizes Cell Tight Junctions to Inhibit Inflammation in Intestinal Epithelial Cells. Salmonella Typhimurium is a major cause of human gastroenteritis.

The Salmonella type III secretory system secretes virulence proteins, called effectors. Effectors are responsible for the change of tight junction (TJ) structure and function in intestinal epithelial cells. The paper sets out the problem first and then the line of work the team chose to take. That makes the article a clear record of one research question, the path taken to test it, and the limits the authors faced.
plos-pone-0002469:
Karkan, working with fellow researchers, published a study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Delara Karkan, Cheryl Pfeifer, Timothy Z. Vitalis, among others. Its subject is a Unique Carrier for Delivery of Therapeutic Compounds beyond the Blood-Brain Barrier.

The piece walks readers through the question, the setup, and the steps that came next. The result is a compact record of the work, of use to readers who study the same problem or teach it to others. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002569:
Pérez-Mancera and fellow authors published a research article through PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Pedro A. Pérez-Mancera, Camino Bermejo-Rodríguez, Manuel Sánchez-Martín, among others. Its subject is fUS-DDIT3 Prevents the Development of Adipocytic Precursors in Liposarcoma by Repressing PPARγ and C/EBPα and Activating eIF4E. FUS-DDIT3 is a chimeric protein generated by the most common chromosomal translocation t(12;16)(q13;p11) linked to liposarcomas.

The paper sets out the problem first and then the line of work the team chose to take. As a record, it keeps the focus on facts and method, and lets readers judge the claims for themselves.
plos-pone-0002669:
In 2008, Joenna Driemeyer and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE about changes in gray matter induced by Learning—Revisited. Authorship is credited in the record to Joenna Driemeyer and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. Recently, activation-dependant structural brain plasticity in humans has been demonstrated in adults after three months of training a visio-motor skill. The article gives specialists and general readers a compact entry point into the topic, with its aims and scope stated up front. No results or figures are claimed in this summary beyond what the title and abstract themselves state.
plos-pone-0002769:
Ulrich Meinzer and others wrote for PLOS ONE in 2008 on the subject of nod2 mediates susceptibility to yersinia pseudotuberculosis in mice. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Ulrich Meinzer, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. Nucleotide oligomerisation domain 2 (NOD2) is a component of the innate immunity known to be involved in the homeostasis of Peyer patches (PPs) in. A further point appears in the abstract. However, little is known about its role during gut infection in vivo . Readers get a clear record of the question, the approach named in the abstract, and the context the authors give for the work.
plos-pone-0002869:
Nasir Salam, Shashank Gupta, Sachin Sharma and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on protection against tuberculosis. Their focus was dendritic cells, a type of immune cell that helps start T cell responses. They asked how two signal proteins, RANTES and IP-10, shape that protection when cells are treated with the bacterial protein CFP-10.

The work looks at how treated dendritic cells prime T cells and guide immune responses to mycobacteria. It links chemokine and cytokine signals to the strength of the response. Readers get a lab-based view of one route the immune system may use to fight Mycobacterium tuberculosis, the germ that causes tuberculosis.
plos-pone-0002969:
Cathrin Bruederle, Robert Hnasko, Thomas Kraemer and co-authors tested whether prion-infected meat-and-bone meal stays infectious after biodiesel production in 2008. The BSE epidemic had collapsed markets for beef by-products such as meat-and-bone meal, a protein-rich feed supplement. Normal rendering did not remove all concern about prions.

A key question was whether turning the fat into biodiesel also destroys infectivity in the remains. The title gives the answer: the meal is still infectious afterward. Published in PLOS ONE, the finding sets a hard limit on one proposed safe use for risky material. The full text gives methods, results, and references for readers who want to check each step.
plos-pone-0003069:
Jean-Marc Melgari, Patrizio Pasqualetti, Flavia Pauri and co-authors mapped upper limb muscles in motor cortex together in 2008. Past work with transcranial magnetic stimulation focused on the cortical representation of a limited group of muscles. No attempt had recorded hand, forearm, and arm at once to disentangle a functional topography.

Their concert metaphor means muscles mapped as an ensemble, not soloists. Published in PLOS ONE, a joint map shows how the primary motor cortex organizes coordinated limb control. That matters for stroke rehabilitation, where recovery is about combined actions, not single muscles. The complete article sets out the methods and data behind each claim in full.
plos-pone-0003169:
Hugo Merchant, Wilbert Zarco, Ramon Bartolo and colleagues examine how timing tasks relate to each other in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. They measured performance links among ten different tasks that involved judging time intervals below one second, using multidimensional analyses. Twenty human subjects carried out explicit timing tasks such as interval categorization.

The authors argue that the context of temporal processing shows up in the pattern of links between tasks. Readers learn that timing is not one single skill but a set of related abilities. That view matters for brain research on time, music, speech, and movement control.
plos-pone-0003269:
Petra Vetter, Brian Butterworth and Bahador Bahrami test a classic claim about counting small sets in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Traditionally, visual enumeration of a small number of items, from one to about four, called subitizing, has been thought of as a parallel, pre-attentive process distinct from serial counting of larger numbers. The team tested this hypothesis by modulating attentional load.

The title reports that attentional load affects numerosity estimation, as evidence against a pre-attentive subitizing mechanism. Readers see a neat textbook split challenged by experiment. How we judge number at a glance matters for models of basic cognition.
plos-pone-0007469:
Jason Ernst and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on how growth signals shape developing blood cells. The growth factor IL-3 keeps early blood progenitors alive and growing. A cancer-causing form of the Abl protein drives similar effects in leukemia. Both were thought to act mainly by switching genes on or off. The team tested a different layer of control.

They found that IL-3 and oncogenic Abl reshape the myeloblast's message pool by changing how long messenger RNAs survive. Altering message stability changes which proteins get made, without touching the genes themselves. That lever turns out to be powerful in deciding a blood cell's fate. Leukemia appears to exploit the same mechanism. The study widens the view of how signals rewrite a cell.
plos-pone-0007569:
Lance Martin, Austin Che, and Drew Endy published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on tools for synthetic biology. Engineers of living systems need standard parts whose behavior is measured precisely. Reporter proteins supply the readouts: some produce color through enzyme activity, others glow. Each kind has strengths and blind spots. The team built a reporter called Gemini that does both jobs in one molecule.

Gemini is bifunctional, acting as an enzymatic and a fluorescent reporter of gene expression at once. Two readouts from one part cross-check each other. That makes part characterization cleaner and more quantitative. Standardized, well-measured parts are the foundation of serious bioengineering. The study contributes a versatile instrument to that foundation. It is a tool paper, aimed at everyone building with genes.
plos-pone-0007669:
Christina Roland and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on what anti-VEGF cancer drugs do besides starving tumors. Blocking VEGF cuts off the growth of blood vessels in solid tumors. Its effects, though, extend into the tumor's immune landscape. No study had compared mechanistically different anti-VEGF inhibitors on tumor growth and environment together. The team ran that comparison in preclinical mouse models of breast cancer, tracking cytokines and immune cell infiltration.

Cytokine levels correlated with how many immune cells entered the tumors. Different blockers shifted that landscape in their own ways. So these drugs are partly immune drugs, whether intended or not. That matters for combining them with immunotherapy. It also gives doctors possible markers for whether the drug is working. The study widens the frame around a well-known class of cancer medicine.
plos-pone-0007769:
Luke Meredith and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It describes a mutant protein that strongly blocks HIV replication. The protein is Tat, which HIV normally needs to copy itself at full speed. The mutant is named Nullbasic.

The team built Nullbasic by swapping Tat's arginine-rich basic region for simple building blocks. The mutant does not just fail to help the virus. It actively inhibits several steps of the viral cycle. A blocker drawn from the virus's own machinery is an appealing drug idea. Proteins like Nullbasic could anchor a new class of HIV therapy.
plos-pone-0007869:
Bo Bai and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It studies the brain's resident immune cells and their effect on T cells. The central nervous system is often called an immune-privileged site. Which cells present antigens there, and how, was largely unknown.

Microglia are the brain's own immune sentinels. The team also made microglia-like cells from dendritic cells in the lab. Both cell types inhibited the proliferation of CD4 T cells. That brake may help keep the brain's immune activity in check. Understanding it matters for brain inflammation and autoimmune attacks on the nervous system.
plos-pone-0007969:
Yudi Pawitan and colleagues asked how many gene variants are still out there to find, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Genome-wide hunts had turned up many variants, but each explained only a sliver of disease risk. The open question was how much more the same approach could yield.

Using the math of what had been found so far, the team forecast the likely haul ahead and the study sizes it would take. Most variants left to find have tiny effects, so the sample sizes must grow very large. The forecast helped funders and teams set honest hopes for the gene-hunting era.
plos-pone-0008069:
Sheila Vinton and colleagues read old plant remains to see how empire changed dinner in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their sites sit in Chile's Atacama Desert, drawn into the Inka empire centuries ago. Studies of conquest often track disease and hunger; this one tracked the household table.

Seeds and other plant traces from homes showed diets shifting as Inka rule took hold. New crops and state demands changed what families grew and ate. The humble seed record thus tells a political story: empire reaches all the way into the cooking pot.
plos-pone-0008169:
Kathryn Whetten and colleagues compared the lives of orphans in institutions and in community care across five poorer nations in PLOS ONE in 2009. The world holds well over a hundred million orphans and abandoned children. Policy had swung toward moving children out of institutions into family settings fast, on thin proof.

Children aged six to twelve were compared on health, feelings, learning, and behavior in both settings. The gaps were smaller, and more mixed, than the policy swing assumed. Care quality, the authors stress, may matter more than the label on the door, a call for proof over fashion.
plos-pone-0008269:
Nina Bosch and colleagues studied a flipped DNA segment in humans in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. A region on chromosome 8, called 8p23.1, can sit in two orientations. This inversion spans several million DNA letters and varies among individuals. Finding markers tied to the orientation helps track who carries which form. The team examined the inversion at several levels.

They assessed its effects on DNA sequence, cell structure, and gene expression. A large inversion can shuffle how nearby genes behave. Knowing its impact helps interpret genome scans for disease. It also adds to the map of human structural variation.
plos-pone-0008369:
Ping-Pui Wong, Adam Pickard, and Dennis J. McCance studied skin cell growth in a PLOS ONE paper from 2010. The protein p300 acts as a transcriptional co-activator in cells. It regulates responses such as growth, transformation, and differentiation. p300 affects the tumor suppressor p53, which controls the cell cycle brake p21. The role of p300 in keratinocyte behavior was their focus.

They found p300 alters keratinocyte growth and differentiation through p21 regulation. Keratinocytes are the main cells of the outer skin. Balancing their growth and maturation keeps skin healthy. The findings link a general co-activator to skin-specific outcomes.
plos-pone-0008469:
Raymond Chan and co-authors revisit brain signs in schizophrenia in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Neurological soft signs are mild flaws in movement or senses. They are common in schizophrenia, as are flaws in thinking skills. Past studies linked the two sets of flaws. But the links were based on simple correlations. The team use a stronger modeling design.

Structural equation modeling lets them test how signs and skills relate. They sort which thinking skills track with which signs. The results give a cleaner map of the links. Such a map may help track illness and sort patients for care and research.
plos-pone-0008569:
Lynda Li Song and co-authors study a protein induced by interferon in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. The protein is called IFI16. Its levels rise in normal prostate cells as they enter senescence. Senescence is the state where old cells stop dividing. IFI16 also slows cell growth. The team ask how it does so at the gene level. They focus on the gene for telomerase, called hTERT.

IFI16 lowers expression of the hTERT gene. Telomerase keeps chromosome ends intact and is switched back on in most cancers. Lowering it helps lock in the growth stop of old cells. The work links an interferon signal to a key cancer gene.
plos-pone-0008669:
Michael Cusimano and co-authors map violent injury in a city in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Injury related to violent acts is a problem in every society. Some authors examined the geography of violent crime. Few focused on spatio-temporal patterns of violent injury. None had used an ambulance dataset to explore its spatial characteristics. The team analyze ambulance records for urban violent injuries over time.

They find violent injury clusters in specific places and times. Hot spots concentrate on certain streets, nights, and hours. Ambulance data reveal patterns police reports may miss. Prevention resources can target those hot spots for greatest effect.
plos-pone-0008769:
Jim Sun, Xuetao Wang, Alice Lau, and colleagues found how the tuberculosis germ stalls its own digestion. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Macrophages swallow germs into sacs called phagosomes. A mature sac fuses with acid-filled lysosomes and kills its cargo. Mycobacterium tuberculosis blocks that fusion and survives inside. The blocking tool was the mystery addressed here.

A germ enzyme, nucleoside diphosphate kinase, proved able to block maturation. Mouse macrophages carrying the germ showed stalled sacs. Removing that block could let macrophages finish the kill. The enzyme becomes a candidate target for new tuberculosis drugs.
plos-pone-0008869:
Nagore Puente, Izaskun Elezgarai, Mathieu Lafourcade, and colleagues mapped cannabis receptors in a small brain hub tied to stress and reward. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The bed nucleus of the stria terminalis helps drive reward seeking and stress responses. The body's own cannabis system influences both behaviors. Yet the system's anatomy inside this hub was barely described. The CB1 receptor is its main brain docking site.

Detailed mapping showed where CB1 sits in the hub's front-side division. Functional tests matched the wiring to behavior circuits. A precise map supports work on addiction and anxiety. It shows where cannabis-like drugs act in this hub.
plos-pone-0008969:
Elvir Becirovic and co-authors traced what one spelling error in a gene does to its message, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Retinitis pigmentosa is an inherited disease that slowly destroys the eye's light sensors. Vision fades over years and can end in blindness. Some cases come from faults in CNGB1, a gene for a channel protein in rod cells.

The team studied one CNGB1 mutation found in patients. The fault sits at a spot where the gene's message is cut and rejoined. Because of it, a whole section, exon 32, is skipped in the finished message. Losing that piece explains how the mutation breaks the channel and harms sight.
plos-pone-0009069:
Weibin Zha and co-authors tested a plant compound against a side effect of HIV drugs, in PLOS ONE in 2010. HIV protease inhibitors save lives but inflame blood vessels over time. That inflammation feeds the lipid problems and heart risks seen in patients. Berberine, a traditional herbal medicine, was the candidate remedy.

In mouse macrophages, berberine calmed the drug-triggered inflammation. It worked by tuning stress signals inside the cells' protein-folding compartment. Those ER stress pathways link the protease inhibitors to the inflammatory response. A plant compound easing drug side effects could widen HIV treatment options.
plos-pone-0009169:
Bob Zimmermann and co-authors watched a molecular fishing contest round by round with deep sequencing, in PLOS ONE in 2010. SELEX is a lab method that evolves DNA strands binding a chosen target. Genomic SELEX fishes such binding strands straight out of a genome. Until now, only the final winners of the contest got read and studied.

Fast, cheap sequencing let the team check the pool after every round. Their neutral version of the method watched strands without forcing a contest. Families of binding strands appeared and faded across the rounds in full view. Tracking the whole process turns a black-box hunt into something observable.
plos-pone-0009269:
Arthur Samuel and co-authors published this virus genome study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Avian paramyxoviruses are bird viruses divided into nine serotypes. By 2010, every serotype's genome had been fully read except type 5. The team filled that last gap.

They sequenced the complete genome of the APMV-5 prototype strain, taken from a budgerigar in Kunitachi in 1974. With it, the set of all nine serotypes is complete. Type 5 turned out to have the longest genome of the group. A complete set lets virologists compare the whole family and trace how these bird viruses evolved.
plos-pone-0009369:
Jonathan Zuccolo and co-authors published this gene family study in PLOS ONE in 2010. The MS4A family includes CD20, a famous target of lymphoma drugs. At least thirteen related genes sit together in the human genome. Most make membrane proteins that span the cell surface four times. A second family, TMEM176, is closely related.

The team traced the evolutionary history of both families. Family trees show when each gene arose and how they spread across species. Such history helps guess what the lesser-known members do. It also explains why some of these proteins became such useful drug targets.
plos-pone-0011469:
Marta Szajnik and co-authors showed in 2010 how tumors recruit the immune system's peacekeepers by mail. Regulatory T cells calm immune attack, and cancers thrive when these cells gather around them. Tumors shed tiny packages called microvesicles into their surroundings, and the team tested what those packages do to human regulatory T cells.

The tumor packages induced new regulatory cells, expanded existing ones, and raised their suppressive activity. In effect, the tumor mails out instructions that build and arm its own bodyguard force. Exposing that trick matters because it names a step that treatment could interrupt: block the packages or their message, and the tumor's shield thins. The study also explains a long-noted puzzle, why regulatory cells are so plentiful and active in people with cancer.
plos-pone-0011569:
Caterina Scoglio and co-authors modeled in 2010 how to fight epidemics where help is far away. Rural regions face outbreaks with few hospitals, long distances, and thin staffing, so strategies copied from cities waste their scarcest resource, time. The team built models of epidemics in rural settings and compared mitigation strategies for efficiency: which measures slow spread most per unit of effort.

Their simulations give public health planners a playbook for the places pandemics hit hardest and help reaches last. Efficient choices might mean protecting transport hubs and clinics first, rather than spreading effort evenly across a map. Modeling before an emergency is the only way to have such answers ready, since mid-outbreak there is no time to compute them. The study treats distance and scarcity as design constraints, not as afterthoughts.
plos-pone-0011669:
Phing-How Lou and co-authors engineered mice that make extra amounts of a hormone-binding protein, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Leptin is a hormone that reports the body's fat stores. Its soluble receptor, OBRe, floats in the blood, binds leptin and adjusts how much of the hormone stays in circulation.

Mice overproducing OBRe weighed less and burned more energy than normal mice. That leaner, faster-burning profile was notable because simply mopping up a hormone might have been expected to blunt its signal instead. The result reveals an unexpected dial on body weight that could inform obesity research.
plos-pone-0011769:
Darius Moharregh-Khiabani and co-authors tested a hopeful multiple sclerosis drug in mice, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Fumaric acid esters were being studied as a pill treatment for the relapsing-remitting form of the disease. One proposed action was direct protection of nerve tissue, beyond calming the immune attack.

The team used cuprizone, a chemical that strips the myelin coats from mouse nerves, to model both the stripping and the repair. They then checked how fumaric acids changed the damage and the regrowth. The test probes whether this drug family can help nerves rewrap, a goal current MS drugs barely reach.
plos-pone-0011869:
Rakel Carpintero and co-workers showed in 2010 that HDL, the so-called good cholesterol particle, can calm a route to inflammation. Small vesicles shed by activated T cells can bind to monocytes, another immune cell type, and trigger them to release inflammatory cytokines. Direct cell contact of this kind is thought to feed diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis.

HDL interfered with that binding, and the monocytes then produced less of the inflammatory output. The finding adds an immune role to a particle known mainly for carrying cholesterol. It also suggests a specific step, vesicle binding, where the calming effect of HDL could be studied for use in inflammatory disease.
plos-pone-0011969:
Ernesto Bernal-Mizrachi and co-workers showed in 2010 that pushing a calcium-driven enzyme too hard in insulin-making cells backfires. Glucose raises calcium in beta cells, and calcium switches on growth pathways that maintain beta cell mass. One key effector is calcineurin, an enzyme activated by calcium and calmodulin.

In mice engineered for extra active calcineurin in beta cells, beta cell mass fell and blood sugar rose, the opposite of the intended growth effect. More signal is not always better; the pathway appears tuned to a middle range. That caution applies directly to diabetes drug ideas built on boosting this pathway.
plos-pone-0012069:
Prasad Burra, Lajos Kalmar, and Peter Tompa found in 2010 that germs fit for great heat run plainer proteins than their mild-weather kin. Such germs grow well at heats from chill to the boil. Much past work told how their stiff proteins hold up in the heat. What had been missed is the floppy side of proteins: the loose parts with no fixed shape that many proteins carry.

Reading gene sets across the full range of growth heats, the team found less of that floppy build. The heat-fit kinds also ran a plainer set of jobs. Loose parts pay off in mild climes but cost too much when heat shakes all parts hard. The trend shows life's slow hand trimming give and flex as the price of a hot home.
plos-pone-0012169:
Colleen O'Rourke, Todd Pitlik, Melissa Hoover, and co-authors compared how day-hunting raptors scan for prey, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Hawks and their kin often hunt from a perch. They watch the ground below for movement. With eyes set on the sides of the head, each bird must move its head in a set pattern. That pattern keeps the scene covered. Yet how the patterns differ between species was little known.

The team measured head movements across raptor species as they scanned from perches. The gaps in rhythm and sweep may match each bird's prey and habitat. Such details show how sight and hunting style evolve together. They can even inform the design of scanning sensors on machines.
plos-pone-0012269:
Gustavo Gómez and Vicente Pallás reported foreign messages traveling into plant chloroplasts, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Chloroplasts, the green engines of plant cells, descend from captured bacteria, and most of their ancestral genes long ago moved into the cell's nucleus. Traffic between nucleus and chloroplast is therefore constant and vital, carried mostly by proteins.

Their finding adds a new courier: noncoding RNA can escort a foreign RNA message into chloroplasts. A signaling route nobody had charted changes how plant scientists think the cell's compartments negotiate. It may also give crop engineers a way to deliver instructions into the chloroplast, a prized target for improving photosynthesis.
plos-pone-0012369:
Nadezhda Tikhmyanova, Alexei Tulin and Fabrice Roegiers studied a fruit fly protein called Dcas in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper on development. Cas proteins in mammals guide cell movement, division, and survival, and they often go wrong in cancer. With four similar Cas proteins in mammals, their jobs blur together, so the team turned to the fly, which has just one.

In fly tissues, Dcas helped cells keep their orientation and supported the adhesion complexes that hold cells to each other. Losing it disrupted growing structures. Because the fly version is simpler, these results clarify what the whole Cas family does, knowledge that feeds back into cancer and development research in humans.
plos-pone-0012469:
Cristina Cellurale, Claire Weston, Judith Reilly and colleagues tested a stress pathway in a mouse breast cancer model, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. The pathway centers on JNK, a kinase switched on by cell stress, and it had been implicated in mammary tumor growth. Their model removes Trp53, the mouse version of the p53 tumor guard, in breast tissue.

By also removing JNK in that setting, the team measured how much the pathway matters for tumors to start and grow. Dissecting one pathway inside a defined cancer model shows whether blocking it could ever help patients. JNK blockers exist, so a clear answer guides drug development for breast cancer.
plos-pone-0012569:
Christian Scherling, Christiane Roscher, Patrick Giavalisco and colleagues used metabolomics to read how plant diversity affects individual species, in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. Diverse grasslands usually produce more total biomass, yet for any single plant species the effect of neighbors can swing from help to harm. Yield totals hide those private fortunes, so the team profiled plant chemistry instead.

Metabolic fingerprints showed contrasting effects of biodiversity on different species sharing the same plots. Chemistry reveals stress and prosperity that weighing plants cannot. The approach may explain why diversity helps fields and meadows overall while individual species rise and fall within them.
plos-pone-0012669:
Feliziani, Lujan, Moyano and co-authors tracked how a lung bacterium changes during long cystic fibrosis infections. Pseudomonas aeruginosa settles into the airways of these patients for years. To survive, it mutates in set genes, gaining traits such as a slimy coat and drug resistance.

Their 2010 study links slime production, cell-to-cell signalling, DNA repair faults and resistance in bacteria taken from chronic infections. The mix shows adaptation is a package, not single changes. Knowing the package helps doctors expect how infections will evolve under treatment and why late-stage infections are so hard to clear.
plos-pone-0012769:
Fuss, Ben Abdallah, Hensley and co-authors reversed a common story about running, new brain cells and anxiety in mice. Running spurs the growth of new neurons in the hippocampus, a brain area tied to mood. Some evidence had cast that growth as calming, yet their 2010 study reports the opposite pattern.

When they used radiation to erase the running-induced new neurons, the anxious behaviour that running produced also disappeared. So in their setup the new cells were needed for anxiety, not against it. The surprise warns against simple claims that more new neurons always mean better mood.
pmc-10869269:
van Kempen, Kim, Tumescheit, and co-authors present Foldseek, a fast way to search by protein shape. Computer methods now predict millions of protein shapes, and that flood has made searching them slow. Knowing a protein's shape helps reveal what it does, so search speed matters.

Foldseek compares a query shape against huge databases by encoding how amino acids touch in three dimensions. That encoding lets it find matches far faster than older shape tools. Quick shape search helps scientists spot distant relatives of a protein and guess at roles for proteins never studied in a lab.
pmc-4267669:
Brinkman, Chen, Amendola, and their co-authors described a simple way in 2014 to measure genome editing results. Editing methods can work well or weakly depending on the target sequence, and the mix of mutations varies too. Labs needed a quick assay to measure what an edit actually did.

Their method, called TIDE, reads the mixed signal in a normal sequence trace and breaks it into its parts. From that breakdown, users can estimate how many cells carry each induced mutation. No special equipment beyond standard sequencing is needed. A cheap, fast check like this helps labs tune editing conditions before moving to costly follow-up work.
pmc-4489269:
Bailey, Johnson, Grant, and their co-authors presented the MEME Suite in 2015. The suite gathers web tools for finding and describing motifs in proteins, DNA, and RNA. A motif is a short pattern that recurs because it carries a biological function.

Finding and describing motifs matters for understanding molecular interactions in the cell. Proteins bind DNA at motif sites, and those sites switch genes on and off. The suite lets users discover motifs in their own data and scan sequences for known ones. It has become a standard resource for labs studying gene regulation across many species.
pmc-4967469:
Iorio, Knijnenburg, Vis, and their team mapped pharmacogenomic interactions in cancer in 2016. Systematic studies of cancer genomes had given unprecedented insight into the molecular nature of cancer. Using that knowledge to guide therapy in the clinic, however, remained challenging.

The team studied how cancer-driven alterations, found across many tumor types, change a cell's response to drugs. They combined genome data with large drug screens in cancer cell lines. The resulting landscape shows which mutations make a tumor sensitive or resistant to specific compounds. Such maps help oncologists match patients to drugs and help researchers design smarter trials.
pmc-5215069:
The Japanese Gastric Cancer Association issued its gastric cancer treatment guidelines in 2014, version four of the document. Gastric cancer, cancer of the stomach, is a major cause of death in Japan, and Japanese specialists have long set standards for its care. National guidelines align surgeons and oncologists on best practice.

A treatment guideline of this kind sets out how the disease should be staged, operated on, and treated with drugs at each stage. It distills trial evidence and expert consensus into clear rules for daily practice. Version updates matter because surgery methods and drug regimens improve over time. Hospitals across Japan base stomach cancer care on this document.
pmc-5431369:
Cappello, Marchetti, Parlanti, and their colleagues characterized the lower motor system in 2016 in a mouse model of Krabbe disease. Krabbe disease is a neurodegenerative disorder caused by lack of a key enzyme's activity. A toxic compound then accumulates widely in neuronal, myelinating, and endothelial cells.

Twitcher mice are widely used as experimental models of this disease. The team used ultrastructural methods, imaging at very fine scale, to describe damage in the lower motor system of these mice. Motor pathways matter because weakness is a core burden of the disease. Detailed maps of cell damage help judge whether new therapies truly protect the nervous system.
pmc-5514969:
Mokhtari, Homayouni, Baluch, and their co-authors reviewed combination therapy in cancer in 2017. Combination therapy treats cancer with two or more drugs at once, and it is a cornerstone of modern care. Pairing drugs is now standard in many regimens rather than an exception.

Using drugs together works better than relying on one drug alone. Combinations target key pathways in a synergistic way, hitting the tumor at several points at once. They can also slow resistance, since a cancer must evade several drugs simultaneously. The review covers the rationale, main strategies, and challenges such as added side effects. It guides clinicians who must design regimens for hard-to-treat cancers.
pmc-553969:
Slater and Birney wrote in 2005 on faster ways to compare biological sequences. Exact alignment methods are sound but slow. Fast shortcut methods run quickly, yet they are hard to build well and their shortcuts are hard to tune by hand.

The authors present a method that bounds a sparse form of the exact calculation, so a quick run stays close to the exact answer. It also lets a program build its own shortcut rules for a given task, rather than rely on rules set by hand. Fast, close alignment is the base of genome annotation and database search. The work fed into tools that compare genes across species at genome scale.
pmc-5573769:
The GBD 2015 Chronic Respiratory Disease Collaborators reported in 2017 on chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and asthma worldwide. These two chronic respiratory diseases are common, with a heterogeneous distribution across the world. The team presents methods and estimates from the Global Burden of Disease 2015 study.

They estimate deaths, prevalence, and disability measures for both diseases from 1990 to 2015. Smoking, air pollution, and occupational dust drive much of the obstructive lung disease burden. Asthma adds a large burden of years lived with disability, including in children. Comparable global figures help countries plan inhaler access, tobacco control, and clean air policy.
pmc-5635569:
Masnoon, Shakib, Kalisch-Ellett, and their team reviewed how polypharmacy is defined in 2017. Older people often live with several long-term health problems at once. That brings the use of many medicines at the same time, a state called polypharmacy.

For all its wide use, the term had no agreed definition. The team ran a systematic review to find and sum up the definitions used in past work. Some counts set a threshold number of drugs; others judge whether each drug is truly needed. A shared term would let studies of risk and benefit be compared. It is a first step to safer prescribing for older adults on long drug lists.

Zihong Chen leads a team of eight hunting genetic risk markers for myasthenia gravis, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The disease weakens muscles when the immune system attacks the junctions where nerves meet muscle. The authors focused on markers inside long noncoding RNA regions, an understudied corner of the genome. They screened candidates from large genetic datasets. Overall, marker frequencies looked alike in patients and controls. Masaki Chujyo, Shu Liu, and Fujio Toriumi ask where a network is weakest when damage spreads outward from a single point, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Such localized attacks, a fire, a flood, a failure cascading to neighbors, threaten power grids and transport webs. Standard importance scores rank nodes by connections, but the authors suspected they miss how position shapes a spreading failure. They propose an index that simulates an attack starting at each node and counts the links severed along the way.

On synthetic and real world networks, their index tracked the actual loss of robustness more closely than the classic centrality measures of degree, closeness, and betweenness. Highly connected nodes were not always the dangerous seeds; shape and neighborhood layout mattered as much. For operators hardening real infrastructure, the index offers a sharper way to decide which single points deserve protection first.

Katherine Van Koevering, Yiquan Hong, and Jon Kleinberg study how Reddit organized itself around COVID-19 almost overnight, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Most big discussion topics accrete communities over years; this one arrived abruptly and hundreds of forums formed within weeks. Using a nearly complete census of those communities, the authors ask what people talked about, who they talked with, and what shapes the self assembly took.

The new forums did not float free of older ones. They plugged into existing frames, political, skeptical, and geographic, and geography proved the single largest organizing theme, despite the crisis being planetary. Neighbors wanted to talk to neighbors about local rules, risks, and resources. The authors call the pattern social tectonics: under sudden pressure, online society snaps into plates along old fault lines, and any emergency communication strategy should expect local identity to dominate.

Cell size and wall thickness together explained most of the variation in bending strength, and the same pair dominated the mass results in swapped order. The catch is that the geometry favoring maximum strength was not the geometry favoring minimum weight. The authors therefore blend the two analyses into a compromise setting rather than crowning a single winner. Their method suits any printed structure, from drone frames to furniture, where grams and strength must be bought together.
