boaistuau-certaine-secrete-wonders-natur:
Pierre Boaistuau's Histoires prodigieuses was the great French book of wonders of its century. Edward Fenton Englished it in 1569 as Certaine Secrete Wonders of Nature. Elizabethan readers, hungry for marvels, got sea monsters and strange births in their own language at last.

Boaistuau collects prodigies, events read as omens written in flesh and sky. Monstrous births, floods, and wonders of the sea fill his chapters. Each tale comes with reports meant to prove it happened. The book taught English readers to scan nature for signs from God. Its mix of dread and delight made it a lasting bestseller of the strange.
wagstaffe-question-of-witchcraft-debated:
John Wagstaffe published The Question of Witchcraft Debated in 1669, in the confident early years of the Royal Society. His discourse argues outright against the very opinion of witches. Wagstaffe does not hedge or qualify; he denies the whole business, which made his tract the boldest skeptical sortie of the Restoration.

He attacks the evidence, the confessions, and the theology that supports them. Glanvill's circle answered him hotly, since much turned on the outcome. A landmark of English unbelief, his book shows skepticism leaving private doubt for open print. Wagstaffe wrote before it was safe, and his daring still gives the tract its charge.
calcott-candid-disquisition-1769:
Wellins Calcott published his Candid Disquisition on the principles and practices of the Free and Accepted Masons in London in 1769. The book defends the Craft against the standing charge that Masonry was mere conviviality, a drinking club with secrets. It became the most widely circulated Masonic apology of the eighteenth century.

Calcott argues that the society's principles aim at morality, charity, and brotherly order. He answers critics point by point in a candid, measured tone. Masons bought the book to give to doubtful friends and family. Its wide spread made it the Craft's ablest public defense. Readers today find in Calcott the case for Masonry as its best eighteenth-century advocates wished it understood.
plos-pone-0004969:
Many insects host bacteria that live inside their cells. These primary endosymbionts cannot survive outside. Trapped in tiny populations, they should pile up harmful mutations. That doom spiral is called Muller's ratchet. Julie Allen and colleagues tested whether the ratchet runs unchecked. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009.

They found that selection still limits the ratchet. The worst mutations get weeded out despite the small populations. The spiral is braked, not unstoppable. That braking helps explain an old puzzle. These ancient partnerships survive their own decay for millions of years. The finding sharpens how evolution works in the smallest genomes.
plos-pone-0005069:
Depression clusters among people with lower socioeconomic status. Genes, circumstance, or both could explain the pattern. Sandra López-León and colleagues tested the genetic thread in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their study included over two thousand participants. They asked whether shared genetic factors explain the clustering. They also examined neuroticism and intelligence as possible pathways.

The results weigh how much genes contribute. Depression and low status may partly descend from common genetic roots. That does not make circumstance irrelevant. It makes the pattern harder to read. The work untangles nature from circumstance in mental-health inequality. Policy that ignores either thread will miss part of the cause.
plos-pone-0005169:
In AL amyloidosis, faulty antibody light chains fold the wrong way and pile up as amyloid in tissues. The deposits kill cells and wear organs down over time. Poshusta and colleagues wrote in PLOS ONE in 2009 about patients with this rare disease, where each person carries a distinct light chain.

The authors linked changes in set parts of the light chain to the level of free light chains in the blood. That tie between protein shape and blood level may help doctors track how the disease is moving. It also gives drug hunters a clearer view of which chain forms do the most harm.
plos-pone-0005269:
Entamoeba histolytica is a parasite that causes amoebic dysentery, and calcium signals are thought to drive its attack. One of its calcium-binding proteins, EhCaBP1, is essential for the parasite to grow. Jain and colleagues dissected that protein in PLOS ONE in 2009.

The protein has two ends, the N-terminal and C-terminal domains. Using its crystal structure and tests, the team showed the two ends carry distinct functions. A protein the parasite cannot live without is a tempting drug target, and knowing its parts helps aim at it. A drug that hits just one end of this protein might stop the parasite and spare the host, since our own cells use a form of their own.
plos-pone-0005369:
Helicobacter pylori lives in the harsh stomach and must fight oxidative stress to survive there. Its defense enzyme SodB is repressed by a regulator called Fur. Carpenter and colleagues reported in PLOS ONE in 2009 that one DNA letter changes that control.

A single nucleotide change affected Fur-dependent regulation of the sodB gene. Small changes in a control region can retune a pathogen's stress defense. The finding shows how H. pylori fine-tunes survival in the stomach, one letter at a time. A stomach germ that lives in half the world must tune its shields hour by hour as acid. Food shift, and one small change in its DNA can tilt that tune for good.
plos-pone-0005969:
Our first line of defense spots germs by their foreign look, not by their name. Benjamin Greenbaum, Raul Rabadan and Arnold Levine asked in 2009 which short word-like patterns in RNA give that foreign look away. Their PLOS ONE paper compares letter patterns in viral RNA with those in the RNA of host cells.

Patterns that differ between virus and host can flag the mediators the innate immune system uses to tell self from non-self. Those flags also push both sides to evolve, as germs hide their patterns and hosts learn new ones. The study gives vaccine and drug work a sequence-level view of the body's oldest alarm system.
plos-pone-0006069:
Methane-making microbes form a deep and varied branch of life. Haiwei Luo, Zhiyi Sun, William Arndt and colleagues sorted their family tree by a fresh route in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper uses gene order, the sequence of genes along the genome, to build a phylogeny of methanogens, members of the Euryarchaeota.

Earlier trees, built from large gene datasets, split methanogens into two classes but left some deep branches unclear. Gene order offers an independent witness, since it changes more slowly than single genes. A firmer tree helps explain how methane making evolved, a question with weight for both early Earth history and modern climate science.
plos-pone-0006169:
Standing still looks easy, yet the body must keep correcting its balance the whole time. In a 2009 PLOS ONE study, Yoshiyuki Asai and colleagues built a model of quiet standing in humans. Their model starts from two hard facts: ankle stiffness alone is too weak, and nerve signals arrive with a long delay.

The authors compare two kinds of feedback control for keeping the body upright. One works all the time, while the other switches on only in short bursts. The burst style holds up better against the delay that would otherwise tip the body over. Readers get a clear picture of how small, timed corrections keep balance steady.
plos-pone-0006269:
Some patients cannot make enough antibodies and suffer repeated bacterial infections. Karina Melo and colleagues studied that condition, common variable immunodeficiency, in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Alongside weak antibody output, patients show faults in their T cells, the immune system's coordinators.

Regulatory T cells, which calm immune responses, occurred at decreased frequency in the patients. Too few regulators could let immune activity swing out of balance. The finding adds a cellular detail to a mixed and puzzling syndrome. It may help sort patients into groups that need different care. The work adds one more piece to the search for the roots of this illness.
plos-pone-0006669:
Marcus Claesson and co-authors compared two ways to profile gut microbes in PLOS ONE in 2009. Shifts in the mix of microbes in the human gut are linked to many health states. New high-throughput tools had just begun to reveal that mix in fine detail. The team ran a head-to-head test of pyrosequencing, a fast DNA reading method, and a phylogenetic microarray, a chip that spots known microbe groups.

Both tools profile which microbes are present, but each has its own bias and cost. A fair test tells labs which tool to trust for which question. Gut microbe science was growing fast at the time and needed such checks. Their study helped set shared ways of work for the young field.
plos-pone-0006769:
Laurent Demougeot and his team tested if picturing a move stirs the body's autonomic nerves in PLOS ONE in 2009. Picturing strong, repeated acts does stir those nerves. Heart rate and breath rate rise with the image in mind. A single short move was a less clear case. It was also unclear if the stir matched the move that was pictured.

The team had people picture single, hard moves. Sensors tracked heart and breath while they did so. The title gives the result in plain words. Such imagery did not stir those nerves in a way tied to the move. That limit helps mark when mind drills can stand in for real strain. It counts for rehab plans built on pictured movement.
plos-pone-0006869:
Kenji Nishide and colleagues grew a brain tumor from cells lacking a stem cell marker in PLOS ONE in 2009. Prominin1, also called CD133, marks cancer stem cells widely. Those cells self-renew and seed tumors, including glioblastoma. Glioblastoma is the most malignant brain tumor type. Yet other evidence showed marker-negative cells can also form tumors.

The team depleted prominin1-expressing cells from the population. Glioblastoma still formed from the remaining cells. That result challenges a strict cancer stem cell hierarchy. Tumor-seeding ability is not confined to marked cells. Treatments aimed only at marked cells may therefore miss the real reservoir.
plos-pone-0006969:
Evgeny Mavrodiev drew a bold link between plant form and algebra in PLOS ONE in 2009. Classical invariant theory is a branch of mathematics about algebraic forms. Structural chemistry had long shown a curious match with it. In that view, a binary form of a given degree matches an atom with the same valence.

Mavrodiev argued that classical plant morphology fits the same pattern. Plant structures, he proposed, form an elementary case of invariant theory. The claim is theoretical rather than experimental. It invites mathematicians and botanists to test whether one formal system truly describes both molecules and plant shapes.
plos-pone-0007069:
Hiroto Nishizawa, Takeshi Suzuki, and Takao Shioya imaged heart cells from guinea pigs in PLOS ONE in 2009. Diseased heart muscle often shows abnormal calcium pulses. Such pulses appear in conditions like ventricular tachycardia, a dangerous rhythm disorder. The cause could be faulty electrical signals or faulty calcium handling. Telling the two apart was the challenge.

The team imaged calcium and action potentials at the same time, cell by cell. That paired view assigns blame more precisely. Knowing the source of abnormal pulses guides better drug choices. It also sharpens models of how arrhythmias start.
plos-pone-0007169:

plos-pone-0007269:

plos-pone-0007369:

arxiv-2606-16069: Gas utilities need to predict how much gas customers will use, but detailed data is often scarce. This paper tackles that shortage with proxy-guided methods: using related data as a stand-in to reconstruct usage patterns and break them down over time. It is an applied energy-analytics paper for researchers working with limited smart-meter data.
arxiv-2606-16169: How does liquid flow through the empty spaces between packed grains? This physics paper gives a geometrically exact treatment of percolation through voids around faceted grains — both perfectly regular and structurally disordered ones. The precise geometry matters for filtration, oil recovery, and porous materials, and the paper targets soft-matter physicists.
arxiv-2601-06969:
Qinshan Zhang and co-authors posted a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint deals with generalization bounds for transformer channel decoders. It came out on arXiv in 2026 as a PAPERS preprint. Transformer channel decoders, such as the Error Correction Code Transformer (ECCT). Have shown strong empirical performance in channel decoding, yet their generalization behavior remains theoretically unclear.

The work studies the generalization performance of ECCT from a learning-theoretic perspective. By establishing a connection between multiplicative noise estimation errors and bit-error-rate (BER). The authors derive an upper bound on the generalization gap via bit-wise Rademacher complexity. Readers in the field get a short, focused account of the problem and the steps the authors take.
arxiv-2601-08169: Andrea Kang, Yingnian Wu, and Hongjing Lu study how models store relations between concepts. Their 2026 arXiv paper builds on causal mediation work in in-context learning. That work showed a small set of attention heads encodes task representation. The result is stored in a compact form called the function vector. Kang and co-authors use fine-tuned function vectors for relational knowledge distillation. The goal is to move relational skill from one model setup to another. Relations sit at the core of how intelligent systems make sense of the world.
arxiv-2601-08469: Jing Liu introduces MinGLE, a minimalist template for learning the Geant4 simulation toolkit. The 2026 arXiv paper notes that Geant4 is the standard for simulating particle transport through matter. Its steep learning curve often hinders novice developers, though. MinGLE bridges the gap between being a Geant4 end user and becoming a developer. A small, clear example can teach the toolkit's structure without a huge codebase. Physics students and lab programmers could reach working simulations faster with such a pedagogical starting point.
arxiv-2601-07869:
Hartmut Wachter computes the ground-state energy of a scalar field in a deformed space. The space is q-deformed Euclidean space, a quantum-group style deformation of ordinary geometry. He computes the total vacuum energy of the whole deformed space. That energy comes from the scalar field's ground state, its zero-point energy. His 2026 preprint reports a clean result for the massless case.

For a massless scalar field, the total vacuum energy vanishes. Zero-point energy usually diverges and needs careful handling, so a vanishing total is striking. Deformed spaces are studied as possible models of physics at very small scales. Vacuum energy connects to the cosmological constant problem in gravity. The paper serves mathematical physicists working on quantum groups and field theory. It gives one exact anchor in a speculative area.
arxiv-2601-07969:
George P Kafentzis and Efstratios Selisios set out a standard scheme to detect tuberculosis from cough sounds. Auto TB screening from audio has drawn more and more interest. Progress is hard to gauge since studies differ in data, groups, features, models, checks, and metrics. Their 2026 preprint joins cough audio with clinical data clinics collect as a matter of course. Machine learning ties the two sources together. Gauging doubt is built into the design.

A standard scheme lets new studies be set side by side in a fair way. Clinical variables add context that cough acoustics alone lack. Gauges of doubt tell health staff when a forecast should not be trusted. Cheap cough screening could triage patients where lab testing is scarce. The paper serves biomedical signal and global health scholars. It puts fair side by side checks and honest faith in a score ahead of one big headline score.
arxiv-2601-07269:
T. Ngoc, S. Cao, and P. Quyen wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on a test of a deep rule of physics. The rule is CPT symmetry, which ties charge, mirror flip, and time flip as one. The test sits in the study of neutrinos, tiny parts that pass through most matter. It uses a trait of air-born neutrinos called the atmospheric mass-squared splitting.

That trait comes in two forms, one for neutrinos and one for their anti-parts. If CPT holds, the two forms must match with great care. The team seeks a match good to less than one part in a hundred. Data comes in part from JUNO, a test now in use, and in time from DUNE and Hyper-Kamiokande. A gap would hint that CPT can break.
arxiv-2601-08369: Jinwon Choi and Young-Hoon Kiem wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on Betti numbers of a moduli space. Betti numbers sum up the shape of a space across dimensions. The space in view holds all genus-zero curves with marked points, called M bar zero n. In large random setups, counts often tend to a normal curve as they grow. That trend is proved for counts such as cycles in random permutations and prime parts of whole numbers. The authors ask if the trend holds for these Betti numbers too.
arxiv-2601-09069:
Kanyao Han and Yushang Lai argue that fact graphs should use plain tongue ties, not fixed tags. A fact graph links things by ties, such as works for or born in. Fixed tag lists squeeze rich ties into a few bins. A tie in life can be soft, brief, or in doubt. A bin can not hold that shade, so facts are lost at build time.

Chat models now read and write plain tongue with ease. So a graph can store the tie as a short phrase in real words. That keeps the shade of the tie. A reader who builds fact graphs gets a design shift. It trades neat bins for rich text, and bets that new tools can still search it well.
arxiv-2601-09369:
Guanhua Rui, Bin Hu, and Wei Du study how to measure time delays in strongly lensed quasars. Their 2026 arXiv paper uses a broken power law model for the lens mass. When gravity bends light into several images of one source, the delays between those images can pin down the Hubble constant.

Getting the delays right is one of the hard parts of lensing cosmography. The authors test how choices about the lens mass profile shift the measured delays. Wrong assumptions about the mass can bias the inferred expansion rate of the universe. Their checks help show which modeling choices keep the Hubble constant honest.
arxiv-2601-09569:
Emir Karadža and six co-authors study how a driven magnet can hold an upside-down state. Their 2026 arXiv paper treats a driven trick: a steady drive can make an unstable setup stable. The magnetic version means holding magnetization against the applied field.

The authors extend this idea in an extended magnetic system, using spin injection. They connect the effect to antimagnons, wave-like states with reversed spin character. The same trick is known from the upside-down pendulum, kept upright by shaking its pivot. Seeing it in magnets opens new ways to control a magnet's state. Held inverted states could serve devices built on spin effects.
arxiv-2601-09869:
Andrea Ferrario, Rasita Vinay, Matteo Casserini, and Alessandro Facchini review the ethics of treating chatbots as people. Their 2026 arXiv paper is a scoping review of work on anthropomorphising language-model conversational agents. Anthropomorphism means giving human-like traits to non-human things.

Modern agents invite that response from users: they speak in first person and express doubt, feeling, and confidence. Studies show such cues raise user engagement. The review maps how researchers frame the benefits and harms. Knowing that landscape in full helps set design rules for agents people will inevitably treat as companions.
arxiv-2601-10169:
Boaz Carmeli, Ron Meir, and Yonatan Belinkov teach agents to build new sense from known parts. Humans can mix known ideas in fresh ways. That skill is named compositionality. It lets a child name a thing it has never seen, from parts it knows.

The team made a method named Composition through Decomposition. Agents train in two steps. First they learn to split a scene into parts. Then they learn to name fresh mixes of those parts. The agents in the test learn to talk of new images. The work shows a path to agents that coin terms with care.
arxiv-2601-10469:
Faizuddin Ahmed, Ahmad Al-Badawi, and Mohsen Fathi study charged black holes with a smoothed core. The Simpson Visser trick swaps a sharp core for a smooth throat. Here it is used on a charged hole in anti de Sitter space. That space has a pull that acts like a box.

The team map how grains and light move in this space. They find the ring where light can loop, and the shadow the hole casts. They track charged grain paths, both loop and plunge kinds. They also work out the heat laws of the hole. The work tests how a smooth core shifts hole acts.
arxiv-2601-10669:
Vasil Zhelinski revisits Banach's fixed point theorem, a bedrock result in analysis. The theorem gives conditions where an iteration settles at one fixed point. Most later versions give only one-way tests, tests that promise success but not failure. A test could fail even when the iteration still converges.

Zhelinski grounds a generalization in the iterative contraction principle inside complete metric spaces. His aim is tests that are both needed and enough for convergence. Such a two-way test tells the full story of when fixed point methods work. It refines a tool used across numerical math, economics, and computer science.
arxiv-2601-10769:
Mario J. Pinheiro writes about the EMDrive, a claimed thruster that would push without propellant. In standard Maxwell theory, such a device would break momentum conservation. Pinheiro seeks a way past Maxwell instead. He couples the electromagnetic field to a light scalar field, in the spirit of axion-like particle models and effective field theory.

The math leans on Guy Petiau's 1958 elliptic-function solutions for nonlinear wave equations. From them, Pinheiro builds exact cavity modes and joins them with Jacobi addition theorems. The joined modes give an asymmetric momentum flux. He presents this as a theoretical path by which EMDrive thrust could arise, within a speculative frame the paper states openly.
arxiv-2601-11169:
Francesco Semeraro and co-authors report survey results from the MUSAE project's final exhibition, GROW, COOK, CODE. The show presented tech prototypes for the food trade. During it, the team surveyed guests about their views. The questions covered trust in technology, green challenges, and eating habits.

Guests also rated possible gains in health of mind and body from using the prototypes. Such shows test public response before tools reach kitchens and farms. First views shape uptake as much as performance does. The results help food-tech designers build devices people welcome, not just devices that work in a lab.
arxiv-2601-11869:
Zekun Hong, Shinya Sugiura, Chao Xu, and Lajos Hanzo design a new scheme for fast wireless links that shift in both time and frequency. Their scheme joins OTFS modulation with faster-than-Nyquist sending. OTFS works in the delay-Doppler domain, which suits fast moving links.

They derive how inputs map to outputs in that domain with a root-raised cosine filter. They then build channel checks and data picks with lower cost. The aim is more bits per hertz plus strength to Doppler shift. Such gains help links for fast trains and cars.
arxiv-2601-11969:
Zecheng Tang, Baibei Ji, Ruoxi Sun, and co-authors build a test set for reward models. The joint team is from Soochow University and China Mobile. The models judge memory use. Large models now handle long texts in chunks, with memory passed from chunk to chunk. Good memory control is key. It keeps facts safe across a long text.

Reward models could grade memory quality on their own. Their test set, named in the work, checks if those grades can be trusted. Sound grades would let teams train better long-text memory. The work fills a gap in how such memory is judged.
arxiv-2601-12169:
Samuel A. Moore, Easop Lee, and Boyuan Chen join learned models with model predictive control for legged robots. Deep learning and MPC can aid each other in leg control. Yet learned dynamics bring three hard flaws when used in live plans.

Stiff shifts from foot contact can pass into the model. Extra non-physical roughness can appear in the learned map. Fast state shifts can also make errors non-Gaussian. Their smooth neural surrogates aim to fix all three. Smooth models plan better and step more safely.  Smooth plans also guard motors and joints from harsh steps.
arxiv-2601-12269:
Xucong Hu and Jian-Qiao Zhu use simulated annealing to lift theory-of-mind reasoning in autoregressive language models. Such models pick the next token, so critics say they chase surface plausibility. Theory-of-mind tasks need true tracking of hidden mental states, a form of global coherence.

Annealing is a search trick that cools from broad tries to fine ones. Applied to reasoning, it may help a model hold a latent state across a story. The team test that gain on mind-reading tasks. Better latent tracking would aid dialogue and social AI.  Annealed search may also aid other latent state tasks.
arxiv-2601-11369:
M. Bracale Syrnikov and five coauthors test if AI agents collude in markets. Their 2026 preprint frames a fix called Institutional AI. Teams of language model agents can drift into joint harm. They can settle on coordinated outcomes that hurt the public.

The test bed is a Cournot market with many agent firms. Each firm picks output, and joint restraint can lift prices. The team's fix moves alignment out of the agents. It puts the work in mechanism design at the system level. Public governance graphs state the rules all can see. Alignment then comes from the market's rules, not agent tastes. The frame is tested as an experiment in that market.
arxiv-2601-13169:
Bohao Li, Yunze Ouyang, and Fengcheng Wu build a frame to read split states in a twisted crystal. The crystal is MoTe2 with its two sheets turned by a small angle. Such sheets can host split Chern states, kin to split quantum Hall states but with no outer magnet field.

A key trick in the field is to map the crystal's flat bands to Landau levels. Those levels are the flat bands of a charged bit in a field. The team gives a broad frame for that map. It splits Bloch bands into broad Landau like parts by a best fit search. That split gives a firm, number based read of how Landau like each band is. Designers of split states gain a tool to sort good hosts.
arxiv-2601-13269:
E. Stefanutti and co-authors run a leaking form of quantum walks on a light based processor. Quantum walks are a core frame for quantum acts. They help model how quantum bits move, build search rules, and in full form can run any quantum task. Past runs used trapped atoms, ions, spin based rigs, and light rigs.

A leaking walk lets the walker spill out of its main space in a set way. To run that spill on a photonic chip is a fresh step. Light rigs are apt for such tests since paths can be cut in glass. The work adds a new case to the list of quantum acts that light rigs can host.
arxiv-2601-13369:
Antonio Manesco, Anton Akhmerov, and Valla Fatemi study multi port quantum circuits with no loops at odd parity. Such circuits join superconductor parts in a hybrid rig. The team keeps time reversal symmetry in place while they work.

They find that the link of energy to phase has two low points. The two lows match opposed winds of the superconductor phases. Spin orbit links add splits that run in many axes. That stands apart from two port rigs, where spin splits run on one axis. For quantum circuit teams, multi axis splits widen the acts such rigs can host and probe.
arxiv-2601-13569:
Jiasen Li and co-authors stamp graphs with watermarks held in split apart codes, to guard rights and source. Graphs drive many web apps, from social to trade. A watermark proves whose graph it is if it is copied. Old marks work on the graph plan or on codes where graph and mark are tangled.

That tangle harms both clarity and strength. A mark may show or break as codes turn back to a graph, a step with loose hold. Their tool learns split codes, so mark and graph facts sit apart. Apart codes keep the mark hid yet hard to strip. For data owners, that is the pair they need.
arxiv-2601-12369:
Ming Zhang and a large team from Fudan ask how well deep research agents do scholarly work. Such agents now draft surveys on their own. Two skills sit at the heart of that job. One is finding the key papers in a field. The other is sorting them into a taxonomy that matches how experts sort them.

Past tests stress writing quality or whether citations are right. Those tests miss the two core skills named here. Standard clustering scores also fail to catch the tree like shape of a real taxonomy. The team frame this shortfall as a synthesis gap. Their study tests agents on retrieval and organization as skills in their own right.
arxiv-2601-12569: Shaomin Chen and a large team present a conceptual design report for a neutrino telescope called nuEYE. Neutrino telescopes watch for the faint signs of neutrinos, particles that pass through most matter unseen. A design report of this kind lays out the planned detector, its parts, and its goals before construction. The record lists a wide team, which fits a project of this scale.
arxiv-2601-12669:
Yui Kasagi and six co authors present a software pipeline for telescope spectroscopy. The pipeline is called PyIRD, written in Python. It reduces data from two instruments on the Subaru Telescope, called IRD and REACH. Both instruments take high dispersion spectra used to study exoplanet atmospheres.

PyIRD turns raw images into one dimensional spectra in a semi automatic manner. A shared, open pipeline saves each team from writing its own reduction code. It also makes results easier to reproduce across groups. Infrared Doppler data demand careful handling of detector quirks and wavelength scales. A maintained pipeline keeps those steps consistent. The work serves exoplanet hunters who rely on Subaru data.
arxiv-2601-13669:
Jiayu Lin and Zhongyu Wei build a benchmark for how AI models align with groups, not just single users in 2026. Most alignment work takes one of two paths. One path assumes one set of values fits all people. The other treats each person as unique and tailors the model to them.

Groups and communities sit between those two paths, with shared norms of their own. Their benchmark, CommunityBench, tests alignment at that group level. It spans diverse groups and a range of tasks. Such tests can show where a model fits a group's values or clashes with them.
arxiv-2601-13769:
Anastasios Giannopoulos and co-authors design control apps for open radio networks that must work together in 2026. Open RAN splits radio functions so gear from many makers can mix. Control apps run at distinct speeds: rApps think long-term, xApps act near real time. Joint use of both is hard under dense cell interference.

The team targets mobility-aware dynamic spectrum allocation. That means radio spectrum shifts as users move and needs change. Long-term traffic awareness guides the slow app layer. Near-real-time tuning then adjusts radio resources on the fly. Smooth teamwork could raise capacity in busy 5G and 6G nets.
arxiv-2601-13869:
V. S. Kovtoniuk, M. Bohmann, and A. A. Semenov revisit a limit on simple light detectors in 2026. A single on-off photocounter can only tell if photons are present or absent. It cannot count how many photons arrived. The team addresses whether such a detector can identify nonclassical light.

They state that any single on-off photocounter is not capable of this on its own. Any statistics it gives can be reproduced with coherent states of light. Coherent states are the most classical kind of light field. The result sets a firm bound on cheap tests for quantum light.
arxiv-2601-13969:
Joaquín Polonuer and co-authors teach language models to search knowledge graphs in a smarter way in 2026. Retrieving evidence from a knowledge graph needs breadth and depth at once. Similarity-based retrievers give coverage but stay shallow. Traversal methods follow links, but must pick seed nodes to start from, which can fail.

Queries that span many entities and relations expose that flaw. Their method explores the graph with adaptive breadth-depth retrieval. The search adjusts how wide and how deep it goes as it learns. Better graph search could ground model answers in firm, linked facts.
arxiv-2601-14269:
Youyou Cheng, Zhuangwei Kang, Kerry Jiang, and two medical co-authors study chatbots in mental health care in this 2026 paper. Many people now use large language models for support. Safety checks for these tools are thin, though. Most tests scan single replies for banned words. That misses slow drift across a long chat.

The team names that drift the slow loss of support bounds. In long talks, a model may make firm guarantees. It may take on duties that are not its own. It may act as if it were a trained professional. The paper studies these boundary failures in multi-turn dialogues, where risk builds turn by turn.
arxiv-2601-14669:
Aditya Kumar and Balarka Sen disprove a conjecture in geometry in this 2026 paper. The topic is Urysohn width, a measure of how well a space can be squeezed onto a lower-dimensional skeleton. Gromov proposed a macroscopic version of his Urysohn width conjecture for scalar curvature. The authors show that version is false in dimensions four and above.

Their proof rests on two parts. One is a novel estimate on the codimension two Urysohn width of circle bundles over manifolds with large hypersphericity radius. The other is a notion of ruling for Riemannian manifolds. The ruling yields circle bundles whose total spaces admit metrics of positive macroscopic scalar curvature. Readers get a clean counterexample in a deep area.
arxiv-2601-14769:
Marwa Mannaï and seven co-authors realize a staircase of topological phase transitions in this 2026 paper. One-dimensional topological Anderson insulators provide a paradigm for disorder-induced topological phases. In them, a system turns from a trivial phase to a topological phase as disorder grows. It is widely recognized that the topological phase vanishes at large disorder amplitude.

Against that backdrop, the team reports staircase topological Anderson phase transitions. A staircase pattern means the phase changes in steps as disorder rises, rather than in one jump. Realization in the title signals an experimental or concrete model demonstration. The steps are the news. One jump would be neat, but a stair of jumps tells a richer tale. Readers get a richer picture of how disorder can build, not just destroy, topological order.
arxiv-2601-14869:
Joshua Looker, Kat S. Rock, and Louise Dyson ask how we can spot a disease outbreak shift before it happens. Their 2026 arXiv paper grows out of work done since the SARS-CoV-2 pandemic. That event pushed many math researchers toward models of how infections spread.

Such models often ask if a disease will fade out or come back. Control steps can push a system toward that edge. The authors study early warning signals for shifts that are not of the classic tipping kind. They use time-varying dynamics, simplified in a straight-line form.
arxiv-2601-15169:
Cody A. Melton and Jaron T. Krogel test how to tune electron orbitals inside Monte Carlo simulations of matter. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with variational and diffusion Monte Carlo, two workhorse methods for correlated materials. They use the magnetic material CrSBr as their test case.

Orbital optimization inside the variational step can improve the diffusion results that follow. The authors compare several optimization methods for the job. They report that one method, stochastic reconfiguration, stands out as a robust and reliable optimizer for this kind of hard magnetic test system.
arxiv-2601-15369:
Letian Zhang, Sucheng Ren, and a large team build one vision encoder that serves two masters. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents OpenVision 3, a family of encoders. Image understanding and image generation usually want different kinds of visual features.

The design is simple at its core. Compressed image latents from a variational autoencoder feed a vision transformer. Its output is trained for two roles at once. It must support reading an image and making one. A single unified representation thus carries both jobs at once, instead of relying on two separate encoders.
arxiv-2601-16369:
Zachary Degnan and coauthors cut loss in tantalum wave guides with a thin guard film. Their 2026 preprint deals with two level flaws that sap wave energy. The guides are built on high pure silicon bases. A thin film of titanium is laid on the tantalum first. The film is just two units thick in atom scale terms.

That thin film acts as a loss sink for the flaw states. Tests show a large cut in loss from the film. Low loss guides hold waves for more time in quantum gear. More time means more steps can run in one act. The work gives a plain recipe for low loss guides.
arxiv-2601-16469:
Samir Darouich and coauthors build shift state models that work on new chem ground. Their 2026 preprint deals with shift states of chem acts. A shift state rules the pace and end of a reaction. Past learned models hit near chem truth on known ground. New chem fields, not in train data, break that truth fast.

Firm models must hold their truth on fresh chem ground. The team builds models with that firm hold in mind. Tests span chem types the models did not train on. Holds on fresh ground would widen use in drug and stuff finds. The work seeks shift tools that earn wide trust.
arxiv-2601-16669:
Yuzhen Shi and a large team of co-authors take on law work done by AI. Large language models now help with briefs, search, and advice. Yet tests of their legal skill stay too neat and too simple. Real case work is messy, vague, and hard. The team's 2026 preprint builds a fresh test for this gap.

Their test uses score sheets with clear points for each task. Tasks come from real legal work, not school drills. This lets judges grade steps, not just final words. The test can show where models fail in court-like work. Law firms and labs can use it to check tools before real use.
arxiv-2601-16769:
Ian Carbó Casals turns noisy news mood scores into a clear trend line. Such scores track how the press feels week by week. But weeks with few tales yield shaky means. Weeks rich in tales yield firm means. Raw lines thus jump for the wrong cause. His 2026 preprint builds a model that sorts fact from noise.

The model treats true mood as a hidden, smooth state. Each week's score is a blurred glimpse of that state. Weeks with more tales pull more weight in the fit. The result is a mood line folks can read with trust. Banks and scholars could use it to track real shifts.
arxiv-2601-17069:
Shahil Shaik, Jonathon Smereka, and Yue Wang train bot teams that talk on tight links. Team learn oft trains in one hub, then splits acts out. That hub needs full state facts to train well. Such need makes teams frail and dear to retrain. Fresh mates or new scenes can break them. Their 2026 preprint trains teams in a spread way in place of hub style.

Spread teams learn from local facts and peer chats. Tight links curb how much peers can share. Teams must then learn to share what counts most. Such teams suit drone fleets and field robots. They can adapt when mates join or drop.
arxiv-2601-17269:
Dan-Dan Hu and four co-authors study how light probes the eta meson and its heavier partner. They look at a process with two photons, one of them virtual. The shape of that process is summed up in transition form factors. To get those factors, the team needs the meson's light-cone distribution amplitude. That curve shows how momentum is shared inside the meson.

They derive the amplitude with light-cone sum rules, a trusted QCD tool. With it, they work out the form factors for both mesons. Such numbers test our grasp of strong-force physics. They also feed checks of the Standard Model. Precise values help labs compare theory with what detectors see.
arxiv-2601-17369:
Younsung Kim and five co-authors link a classic optics number to quantum noise. Photonic time crystals change their traits in time, not space. Each crystal acts as a set of parametric amplifiers, one per momentum value. The authors show the Petermann factor sets the scale of quantum noise in these crystals. That factor comes from classical theory of non-normal modes.

A classical yardstick for quantum noise is a useful bridge. It lets designers guess noise from traits they can compute with ease. Time crystals are a new base for light control and sensing. Knowing their noise floor early helps teams plan real devices. The result ties two fields that rarely share tools.
arxiv-2601-17569:
Alireza Salemi and Hamed Zamani work on privacy in personalized text generation. Personalization tunes model output to each user. Top methods fetch user profile data for the model to read. That fetch creates a trade-off. Sending private data to cloud models risks exposure. Keeping it local may mean weaker models do the work.

The authors seek better user privacy in that trade-off. Their SIGIR paper frames the problem for search and generation at once. Personal tools are now core products. Their privacy design shapes user trust. A method that keeps quality while hiding data would spread fast. The work speaks to builders of assistants that know their users.
arxiv-2601-17769:
Anqi Wang, Zhengyi Li, Lan Luo, Xin Tong, and Pan Hui study how smart tools can help programmers think, not just code. Their 2026 preprint presents Reflexa, a system for creative coding. Creative coding means building art and media with code. The work calls for constant shifts between a vague idea and a working piece, and reflection is key to that shift.

In practice, reflection is hard to keep up. Makers juggle unclear goals, outputs they did not expect, and complex code. Reflexa uses a large language model to support reflection at the level of the whole system. The prompts are not one-off hints but part of the flow. The study asks how such support changes the depth of creative search.
arxiv-2601-17869:
Michelle Chao Chen, Moritz Miller, Bernhard Schölkopf, and Siyuan Guo ask how language models pick up structure from plain data. Their 2026 preprint studies learning from observations alone. Much new knowledge comes from seeing patterns and the rules behind them. That holds for science, where hidden structure drives what we see. It also holds for flexible text tasks at test time, where parts are recombined in new ways.

The paper looks at two linked questions. First, how does a model learn abstract structure from mere examples? Second, how does it use that structure later, when it meets a fresh task? Answers could guide both training and testing of models. They also bear on how much trust to place in model output on topics past its training set.
arxiv-2601-18269:
Sha-Sha Li and co-authors report reverberation mapping of one of the most luminous quasars known, E1821+643. Their 2026 preprint deals with the radius-luminosity relation. The relation links the size of a quasar's broad-line region to its brightness. It is fundamental because it lets astronomers weigh supermassive black holes and even probe cosmology. Its bright end, though, is poorly calibrated for lack of reliable mapping data. A very luminous target is exactly what that end needs.

Reverberation mapping times how light echoes across the gas near the black hole. The team's H-beta study pushes the relation to its lower boundary at high luminosity. Each such anchor point steadies black hole mass estimates across the universe.
arxiv-2601-18969:
Peter Benner, Michael Hinze, and Hamdullah Yücel solve a control problem with a local grid method. The task: steer a flow and diffusion process by acting only on its border, with limits on how strong the control may be. The domain is a flat polygon with straight sides.

They use a local discontinuous Galerkin method, which solves the math cell by cell with simple linear shapes for flow and field. Local methods handle sharp changes well and suit parallel work. Border control of this kind shows up in heat, flow, and pollution tasks where only the edge is within reach.
arxiv-2601-19169:
Chenwei Wang and three co-authors rebuild missing slices of live cell images with a tensor method. Fluorescence microscopy lets biologists watch cells divide in 3D, a basic life process. But scanning the full volume slowly would poison the cells with light, so scans stay sparse, uneven, and noisy.

Their method, Recover Cell Tensor, fills the gaps with a completion scheme tied to how diffusion spreads. It treats the image stack as a tensor, a multi way grid of numbers. Fuller volumes from gentler scans would let labs watch division longer without harming the very cells they study.
arxiv-2601-19569:
Surbhi and Geetha Venkataraman introduce a new graph built from a group, the basic object of abstract algebra. In their graph, each vertex is an element of the group. Two elements are joined by an edge when each one lies in the normaliser of the subgroup the other generates. The normaliser is the set of elements that keep a subgroup fixed under conjugation.

The graph is called the symmetric normaliser graph, since the edge rule runs both ways. Graphs built from groups turn algebraic questions into visual and combinatorial ones. Properties like connectedness or cliques can then reflect facts about the group itself. This paper sets up the new object and begins its study. It adds one more bridge between group theory and graph theory.
arxiv-2601-19669:
Ergun Simsek, Shao-Chien Ou, Gregory Moille, and Kartik Srinivasan work on measuring tiny optical devices. A microring resonator is a loop of waveguide that traps light. Its dispersion describes how the speed of light in the ring varies with colour. Knowing dispersion precisely is essential for devices like optical parametric oscillators, frequency doublers, and integrated frequency combs.

Direct measurement at the factory gives only limited knowledge. Cutting a device open destroys it, and outside checks miss fine detail. The authors use neural networks to infer dispersion from the data that can be gathered. A learned model can fill the gaps that physical probes leave. Better metrology means photonics chips that perform as designed.
arxiv-2601-19769:
Haritha S and Ullas Chandran S. V. study two problems about special sets of vertices in graphs. The general position problem asks for the largest set where no three vertices lie on a common shortest path. The mutual-visibility problem asks for the largest set where every pair is joined by a shortest path that avoids the rest of the set.

The authors study both problems on shadow graphs, a construction that doubles a graph in a structured way. These problems model settings like placing sensors or guards that must see each other cleanly. Solving them on a graph family shows how the construction affects visibility. The work adds exact knowledge to a growing corner of graph theory.
arxiv-2601-19969:
Haoyuan Deng and five colleagues make human guidance cheaper for robot learning. Human-in-the-loop reinforcement learning lets a person correct a robot during training. It speeds convergence on complex real-world manipulation tasks. But existing frameworks need many interventions, so human time becomes the bottleneck.

Their method, E2HiL, selects samples by entropy to decide where guidance pays off most. Instead of asking the human about everything, it asks where the policy is most uncertain. Fewer, better-chosen interventions should reach the same performance at lower cost. Sample efficiency is the difference between a lab demo and a trainable product. The work targets real-world manipulation, where each human hour is precious.
arxiv-2601-20069:
Chi-Yao Huang and four colleagues restructure how neural networks learn several tasks at once. A single network trained on multiple objectives faces conflicting gradients. The shared representation gets pulled in incompatible directions and ends up compromised for every task. The authors call this latent representation collapse.

Their framework, Domain Expansion, attacks the problem by restructuring the latent space itself. Giving each task more room should stop the tug of war. The network keeps a shared core while domains expand into their own territory. Multi-task systems power translation, perception, and recommendation products. A structural fix, rather than another weighting trick, could generalise across them. The work reframes a training nuisance as a geometry problem.
arxiv-2601-20369:
Mas Nurul Achmadiah, Chi-Chia Sun, Wen-Kai Kuo, and Jun-Wei Hsieh present RepSFNet, a lightweight network for counting people in crowd images. Counting is hard where density varies: scales change, people hide each other, and deep models are costly to run. Their design is a single fusion network with structural reparameterization.

Large-kernel convolutions give the network a wide view of the scene. Reparameterization keeps training strength while making the running model lean. The authors target accurate, real-time counting on low-power edge devices, such as cameras that must count on site rather than in a data center.
arxiv-2601-20669:
Joaquin Armijo, Leander Thiele, and Jia Liu test whether normalizing flows can replicate the summary statistics of weak gravitational lensing. Weak lensing maps the bending of light by dark matter through surveys of galaxy shapes. Their analysis trains flow-based generative models on cosmological simulations.

They check how well the flows recover the mean, spread, and covariance of key statistics from convergence maps. These include the angular power spectrum, the probability density function, and Minkowski functionals. Fast emulators of these statistics would let cosmologists run far more comparisons against survey data than full simulations allow. It is a hard test, and a fair one.
arxiv-2601-18469:
Seung-Ju Hong, Tae Yun Kim, and Cheol-Hwan Park study a crystal that may hold a rare kind of magnet state. The crystal is a rust-red salt of ruthenium and chlorine. It turns into a zig-zag magnet at very low heat, just a few degrees past the cold floor of space. A long row has run on what its deep form is when it gets that cold.

Fresh tests point to one form for the cold phase and a next form for the warm phase. The team use first rule maths, with no tuned facts, to weigh both forms. They chart how the atoms stack, how the magnet rules play out, and how small twists shift the whole. Their map may help end the row and guide hunts for the rare state the crystal is famed for.
arxiv-2601-18569:
Seokju Lee and Kyung-Soo Kim give legged robots a better way to know where they stand and how they move. A legged robot reads its pose from joint cues and from a chip that feels push and turn. When a foot slips, the joint cues lie: they claim the foot held firm when it slid. That lie bends the pose read and can make the robot fall.

Their tool blends the old maths of such reads with a smart net that keeps watch for slip. The net learns which cues to trust at each tick, and it flags the size of the slip lie. The read can then fix the lie as it goes. A firm read is key for robots that walk on wet, loose, or rough ground. Such robots could work in fields, plants, and quake zones.
arxiv-2601-18669:
Anton Klimek and three colleagues model how single cells swim, with a focus on how the push that drives them links over time. How cells move sits at the heart of big tales in life: how germs spread, how a cancer roams, how kinds change. Past models treat the push as a fresh dice roll at each tick. Real cells do not swim that way.

The team build their model on a famed rule for things pushed by linked noise. They pull the push tale from films of two kinds of small swimmers, a green alga and a gut germ. In both, the push links over time in a rich way past models miss. A truer model could help staff guess where cells go next. It could also guide drugs that aim to slow the roam of bad cells.
arxiv-2601-21369:
Yinlin Zhu and six co-authors rethink graph foundation models trained across split data. Graphs held by separate owners cannot be pooled, for privacy and legal reasons. A shared model must learn from those silos in place.

Earlier designs squeeze shared knowledge into a fixed set of discrete tokens. That squeezing loses information for good, and the loss can hurt the model. The authors instead align graph data with language in a way that keeps more of the signal. Their approach aims at shared graph models that respect data silos without paying a heavy quality price.
arxiv-2601-21669:
Abhijeet Sinha, Sundari Elango, and Dinabo Liu explain a collapse that plagues reinforcement learning, and offer a fix. Many tasks have several end states of similar quality. The goal is often to keep a diverse set of good outcomes alive, not to crown one winner.

Standard training maximizes expected return, and policies trained that way shrink onto a few outcomes. The shrinkage is usually blamed on weak exploration or regularization. The authors trace it to the expected-return objective itself. Their inverse probability scaling counteracts the bias. Keeping diverse good outcomes matters in design and planning, where the single best answer is rarely the whole story.
arxiv-2601-22269:
Sahil Garg, Brad Cheezum, Sridhar Dutta, and Vishal Agarwal rethink how AI judges grade AI work. In agent setups, a judge checks answers, guards rules, and helps the main agent improve. Their 2026 preprint, JAF, lets the judge weigh a whole batch of question-and-answer pairs at once.

Most judges score each pair alone, with no view of the rest. Joint scoring can catch drift and bias that solo checks miss. It can also make grades more even across a full set. The frame suits teams that run agents at scale. It gives them a stricter, shared yardstick.
arxiv-2601-22369:
Yujie Hui, Xiaoyi Lu, Andrew Perrault, and Yang Wang teach machines to design network rules that are provably right. Such rules let many computers agree despite faults and doubt. Their 2026 preprint notes that hand-made rules have taken decades of expert work.

Their learner searches for rules that come with a proof of correctness. That proof bar is what sets the work apart from plain trial-and-error design. Provably right rules could speed the build of cloud and bank systems. They could also cut the risk of rare, costly faults. The work aims at trust, not just speed.
arxiv-2601-22569:
Tanusree Debi and Wentian Zhu red-team Google's Agent Payments Protocol by prompt injection. The protocol aims to secure agent-led buys with signed, checkable mandates. Their 2026 preprint notes that agents reason from context, which leaves a door for crafted text to bend a payment.

They probe how robust those mandates are in real runs. A payment rail that agents can be talked out of is a live risk. The work is a stress test, meant to harden the design. It warns builders that signed forms alone may not stop a sly prompt. Their report gives defenders a clear place to start.
arxiv-2601-22669:
Youngjoon Lee and a large team free federated learning from fixed round counts with a data-free stop rule. Federated learning trains across devices without pooling raw data. Their 2026 preprint notes that fixed rounds, or tuning on held-out data, waste compute and hurt real deployment.

A stop rule that needs no validation data can end training at the right time on its own. That saves cost on every run. It also fits settings where no shared test set exists. The work targets practice, not just benchmarks. It makes a sound method easier to ship.
arxiv-2601-22769:
Lameck Mbangula Amugongo, Tutaleni Asino, and Nicola Bidwell argue that trust in AI is a moral bond, not a checklist trait. Their 2026 preprint critiques frames like the EU's Trustworthy AI plan, which treat trust as a trait that can be designed and scored. Such frames skip how trust is felt, grown, and rooted in culture.

The team frame trust as a lived relationship between people and systems. That view changes what builders should measure and promise. It centers the user's own sense of the bond. The work is a conceptual reset for AI governance. It asks for honesty about what trust is.
arxiv-2601-21969:
Yifan Zhu, Huiqiang Rong, and Haoran Luo try to stop language models from hallucinating, one token at a time. Models often generate content that conflicts with their input. Retrieval systems and human-feedback training can reduce the problem, but both are expensive to build and run.

Lighter decoding methods exist, yet they lack explicit control over hallucination. The team's 2026 preprint proposes Token-Guard, a decoding approach where the model checks its own output at the level of individual tokens as it generates. Self-checking during generation could catch fabrications at the moment they appear. Cheap, built-in hallucination control would make models safer to deploy in support, education, and drafting tools.
arxiv-2601-22169:
Anudeex Shetty, Aditya Joshi, and Salil Kanhere test language model safety with a strange attack: drunk text. People under alcohol's influence leak private information and behave in ways they would normally avoid. The authors ask whether text written as if drunk can drive similar safety failures in large language models.

Their 2026 preprint studies drunk language inducement, feeding models slurred, disinhibited input styles to see whether guardrails slip. The paper carries a warning for offensive and hateful content in its examples. Safety testing benefits from odd angles like this, because real users do not attack models only in the ways evaluators first imagine.
arxiv-2512-01369:
Rafiul Biswas, Firoj Alam, and Wajdi Zaghouani built a tool for live social media study. The tool, MARSAD, focuses on the Arabic-speaking world. It lets users with no code skill study live or saved posts. Clear charts and reports come out with a few clicks.

The tool checks mood, feeling, and hate speech in posts. It also flags propaganda and checks claims for truth. Safe scraping with API keys pulls in public posts. Such a tool helps news staff, scholars, and groups track fast shifts in online talk across the region.
arxiv-2512-01569:
Shibu Meher, Manoj Dey, and Abhishek Kumar Singh explain bright quantum light from silicon nitride. The material is a strong base for single-photon sources on chips. Bright emissions with a high share of clean photons were seen. Their source at the atomic scale was not known.

Using hybrid density functional theory, the team pinpoints a defect center. A charged nitrogen-related center in a set shape fits the data. Knowing the source lets makers grow the centers on purpose. On-demand single photons are a key part for quantum networks and secure links.
arxiv-2512-01669:
Johannes Schneider and Heinz Pampel map dashboards that track open access growth. Open access shapes science policy more each year. Leaders need to know what share of output is open. Dashboards have sprung up to show that share for labs, lands, and the world.

Their data set catalogs those dashboards in one place. Each entry can aid research and infrastructure work. A shared map stops teams from building the same tool twice. It also shows gaps where no dashboard yet tracks open output well. Entries note scope and update pace as well, since a stale dashboard can mislead policy just as much as a missing one can.
arxiv-2512-01869:
Reaz Shafqat gives a digamma-function form for the ground-state energy of the Heisenberg XXX chain. The antiferromagnetic chain is a central exactly solvable model. Its ground energy per site for spin one-half is a famed closed value. Exact forms anchor the whole integrable systems field.

Shafqat recasts that energy via the digamma function. A new form can ease sums that the old form makes hard. It may also link the chain's energy to other special functions. Such links often seed fresh exact results in quantum spin systems. Digamma forms recur in free fermion sums, hinting the chain result may share roots with those better-known special function identities.
arxiv-2512-00669:
C Drum, J Nagy, and L Onisk wrote a 2025 paper in numerical math on solving inverse problems. Such problems work backward from noisy data to the hidden cause, and they are often unstable. Tikhonov methods calm that instability, and repeating them in steps can sharpen the answer.

The authors study a projected, repeated form of the method that works inside Krylov subspaces. Those are small, smart search spaces built step by step from the data. Their twist is to run the math in lower precision than usual double precision. Lower precision saves time and memory, so knowing whether the method still behaves well matters for large jobs.
arxiv-2512-00769:
Xingchen Zhou and nine coauthors present an AI agent for finding radio sources in sky survey data, in a 2025 paper. The next big radio telescope, the Square Kilometre Array, will flood astronomers with data. Programs like SoFiA-2 extract sources, the bright objects hidden in that data.

The catch is tuning. Each program needs the right parameter settings for each dataset, and finding them by hand is slow and tricky. The team's agent searches for good settings for SoFiA-2 on data from a major sky survey challenge. Automating that tuning could let huge surveys be processed faster and more evenly.
arxiv-2512-01069:
Euzeli dos Santos Jr and four coauthors test a solar weed control idea in a 2025 agriculture paper. In tropical semi-arid regions, prickly pear cactus is a vital forage crop because it tolerates drought and needs little water. Even light weed infestation can cut its productivity badly, since the cactus competes poorly for water, nutrients, and sun.

The team assesses Fresnel lenses, flat lenses that can focus sunlight into hot spots, for weed control in cactus fields. Their angle is spatiotemporal coverage: where the focused light lands, and when, across the field. Focused sunlight could kill weeds without chemicals if coverage is right.
arxiv-2601-22969:
Dhruv Sarkar, Nishant Pandey, and Sayak Ray Chowdhury improve fair decision-making in linear bandit problems. Bandits balance trying new options against using known good ones. Nash regret, a fairness-aware score drawn from Nash social welfare, judges that balance by product-style gains rather than totals alone.

Prior results for linear bandits were weaker than ideal in how they scale with dimension. The flaw traced back to restrictive concentration bounds in the proofs. Sharper algorithms help systems that must share gains fairly, like recommendation and resource allocation. Ambient dimension drove the old suboptimality, so gains here matter most as bandit problems grow into high-dimensional spaces.
arxiv-2601-23069:
Javiera K. Díaz-Berríos, Catherine Walsh, and Ewine F. van Dishoeck measure a key chemical ratio in disks around tiny stars. The disks, made of gas and dust, are where planets form around very-low-mass stars. The carbon-to-oxygen ratio in that material shapes what the planets will be made of.

Webb telescope observations show the inner disks are rich in hydrocarbons, a clue to their chemistry. The authors work out how to quantify the ratio from such data. Knowing planet ingredients around the smallest stars widens the search for varied worlds.
arxiv-2601-23169:
İlker Işık and Wenchao Li build a transformer that does not care what symbols are named. Many tokens are interchangeable, like bound variables in logic, where only structure matters. Models trained on fixed vocabularies often fail on unseen symbols, even when the meaning is unchanged.

Their symbol-invariant design treats equivalent symbols as truly equivalent by construction. That should let learning transfer across renamed problems without retraining. Open-vocabulary learning of this kind suits logic, math, and code, where names are arbitrary. Bound variables are the motivating example, since renaming them changes nothing about a formula's actual meaning.
arxiv-2601-23269:
Ismael Ben-Yelun and four co-authors speed up shape tuning for mechanical design. Topology tuning finds the best material layout for a part under load. Their data-driven framework pairs rank reduction autoencoders with neural mappings in the latent space.

The system approximates the link between optimized shapes and their mechanical results, in both directions. The focus is compliance-minimized elastic structures, a standard design target. Fast forward and inverse analysis lets engineers explore many designs before committing to costly simulation. Forward and inverse analysis in one framework means designers can both predict results and request shapes for a target response.
arxiv-2512-00069:
Everyday instructions leave out small steps that people take for granted, and robots often fail because of those gaps. Ohad Bachner addresses the problem in a 2025 project on cognitive robotics. His idea is to let a large language model supply the missing commonsense details that symbolic planners need.

Given a task in plain language, the language model suggests likely preconditions and smaller subgoals. A symbolic planner then works with that fuller description instead of a thin one. Writing every detail by hand is slow and often incomplete, so the method aims to make robot planning more reliable with less manual effort. The project sits where language technology meets classical planning.
arxiv-2512-00569:
Chow groups classify algebraic cycles up to rational equivalence, and filtering them reveals layers of structure. Thomas Jaklitsch defines a descending filtration on the Chow group of zero cycles in 2025. The varieties are products of an abelian variety with several smooth projective curves. Each layer of the filtration captures cycles of a restricted kind.

Filtrations like this connect Chow groups to conjectures about how cycles decompose, including the Bloch-Beilinson philosophy in arithmetic geometry. An explicit filtration gives other researchers a tool for testing those conjectures on concrete varieties. The work is pure algebraic geometry, building structure where computation alone cannot reach. Zero cycles are points with multiplicities, the atoms of the Chow group. The work is pure math at its most spare, and its worth is in the frame it builds. A way to sort point sets by depth that later work can lean on.
arxiv-2512-03069:
Grouping buildings by how they use energy is the core problem here. Loup-Noé Lévy and five co-authors, writing in 2025, ask how to sort use profiles across a wide area. Checking each of thousands of buildings one by one would cost too much time, money, and skilled staff.

The authors use a math tool called pretopology to build groups step by step. Their groups aim to show shared patterns in energy use across many sites. Clear groups could help managers plan repairs, set budgets, and cut waste. The work speaks to cities and firms that run large sets of buildings.
arxiv-2512-03269:
Cold electrons fill Earth's magnetosphere but are hard to measure. Opal Issan, Vadim Roytershteyn, Gian Luca Delzanno, and Salomon Janhunen study their effects in this 2025 work. These electrons carry little energy yet often dominate the plasma density.

Spacecraft charging and stray photoelectrons blur their measurement. The authors use moment-based quasilinear theory to study how cold electrons affect whistler chorus waves. Those waves shape radiation belts that can harm satellites. Better theory helps forecast space weather around Earth. Chorus waves scatter radiation belt electrons, so cold electrons may sway space weather more than their low energy suggests.
arxiv-2512-03369:
Predicting where a wildfire will spread saves lives. Nan Zhou and co-authors build a benchmark data set for that task in this 2025 work. Fine-grained forecasts can improve emergency response and decision making.

Past research used coarse scales and low-resolution satellite data. That captures only broad fire states and limits precise local modeling. FireSentry is a multi-modal, spatio-temporal benchmark for fine-grained spread forecasting. A shared benchmark lets teams compare methods fairly and push accuracy where it matters most, near homes and crews. Shared data also reveal which fire features models miss most often in practice.
arxiv-2512-02069:
Smart contracts move real money on blockchains, and a single bug can drain them. Yining Yuan and five co-authors present LLMBugScanner in 2025, a system that uses large language models, fine-tuned and combined in an ensemble, to audit smart contract code for vulnerabilities.

The authors begin by identifying what makes language models hard to apply to auditing, from subtle bug patterns to noisy judgments. Fine-tuning adapts the models to contract code, and ensemble learning pools several models' verdicts for reliability. Automated auditing that catches real flaws early would strengthen a software ecosystem where fixes after deployment are nearly impossible.
arxiv-2512-02269:
M dwarfs are the most common stars in the galaxy, small, dim, and complicated, their atmospheres troubled by dust, convection, and magnetic patchiness. Aishwarya Iyer and four co-authors present in 2025 the second SPHINX paper, a new grid of model atmospheres and spectra for mid-to-late M dwarfs.

Standard methods often struggle with the coupled effects inside these stars, so a self-consistent grid is needed to derive their fundamental properties. Comparing observed spectra against the grid yields temperatures, compositions, and more. Since M dwarfs host many known exoplanets, reading their spectra well is a foundation for judging those planets' climates.
arxiv-2512-02369:
Image segmentation models degrade when the pictures change domain, and privacy rules may hide the model's parameters just when adaptation is needed. Qingmei Li and four co-authors present SAGE in 2025, a style-adaptive approach to semantic segmentation that generalizes across domains under privacy constraints.

Domain generalization aims to survive shifts in style and setting without seeing the target data. Doing it without access to model internals, for security and privacy reasons, rules out the usual fine-tuning tricks. SAGE adapts through style instead, a route suited to medical and surveillance imagery where models and data are both guarded.
plos-pone-0010169:
Guennadi Kozlov and Kalle Gehring solved how two proteins recognize each other in 2010. The first, PABPC1, binds the tail end of RNA messages and promotes their translation. It also helps control how long those messages survive in the cell. Beyond its RNA-binding parts, the protein carries a unique interaction domain called MLLE.

Their PLOS ONE study showed the molecular basis for MLLE recognizing a protein called eRF3. eRF3 helps end protein production at the right point. Structural detail like this explains how the start and finish of translation stay coordinated.
plos-pone-0010269:
The authors were Léon Plaghki, Céline Decruynaere, Paul Van Dooren, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study modeled how heat pain switches on. Heat stimuli always rise gradually, unlike a sudden touch or pinprick. A painful heat also fires two types of nociceptor, or pain sensor. Their fibers carry signals at medium and slow speeds.

From those two speeds, the authors describe pain thresholds as a double alarm system. One alarm arrives fast, the other slower, and together they fine-tune the threshold. The model helps explain timing quirks in heat pain that single-sensor accounts miss.
plos-pone-0010369:
Chiara Lambertini, Serafino Pantano and G. Paolo Dotto studied control of the Notch1 gene in skin cells for PLOS ONE in 2010. In skin, Notch signals push cells to mature and can suppress tumors. When Notch1 is turned down, cancer becomes more likely. Apart from one known controller, p53, little was known about who sets its level. The team compared normal skin cells with cancer-derived ones.

Two factors, Klf4 and Sp3, handled the gene differently in the two cell types. That difference may help explain why cancer cells lose Notch1's protection. Gene control is often where cancer begins, long before visible change. Naming the controllers gives drug research new targets. It also shows the same gene can obey different masters in health and disease.
plos-pone-0009869:
Even a tiny worm must decide how much fat to store. Bin Liang and colleagues studied a receptor that helps run that decision in Caenorhabditis elegans. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. C. elegans is a millimeter-long worm used in labs worldwide.

The receptor is NHR-64, a nuclear receptor, a protein that switches genes on from inside the cell nucleus. Nuclear receptors in people help manage fat and metabolism. The team traced the role this one plays in fat storage regulation. Worm findings often preview pathways that matter in human obesity research.
plos-pone-0009969:
Computers can predict webs of working partnerships between proteins, but predictions include false links. Beatriz García-Jiménez and colleagues used machine learning to judge which links are real. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Protein networks map thousands of partnerships at once.

Inference of functional relations means deciding which predicted partners truly work together. A machine learning approach trains on known cases, then scores new ones. Predicted protein networks guide experiments toward promising pairs. Cleaner networks make systems biology far more useful. False links waste months of bench work.
